Consistently attributed to Twain across quote collections and stylistically plausible for him; I have a weak recollection of it sitting in one of the late novels but cannot place the work or chapter with enough confidence to name it, so I am leaving the print source null rather than guessing. Author plausible, citation unconfirmed.

Widely printed over Twain's name but absent from his writings so far as I know; the Twain attribution surfaces decades after his death, and quote-tracing work on this line has failed to find any contemporaneous support. Related sentiments about kindness as a universal language predate the Twain version. True origin unknown to me.

results.earliest_print_source: Following the Equator, Mark Twain, 1897 (epigraph from Pudd'nhead Wilson's New Calendar)
results.notes: Genuine Twain, one of the Pudd'nhead Wilson's New Calendar chapter epigraphs in Following the Equator. Twain's wording is 'the full value of a joy'; the corpus reads 'of joy'. Correct author, published in his lifetime.

Very consistently attributed to Twain and usually pointed at his notebooks, but I cannot confirm which entry or letter, and I have not seen it quoted with a page citation. Plausible but unconfirmed - keeping it below the promotion bar until someone checks the notebooks.

results.earliest_print_source: "The Computer for the 21st Century", Mark Weiser, Scientific American, September 1991
results.notes: These are the opening two sentences of Weiser's ubiquitous-computing paper, quoted verbatim and correctly. One of the best-documented attributions in computing; the text matches the published article word for word.

results.earliest_print_source: Reflexions et maximes, Luc de Clapiers, marquis de Vauvenargues, 1746
results.notes: The maxim is Vauvenargues': 'Il n'est rien que la peur ne fasse croire,' from his Reflexions et maximes (published 1746 with the Introduction a la connaissance de l'esprit humain). The author field is misspelled and mistitled - it should read 'Luc de Clapiers, marquis de Vauvenargues', not 'Marquis de Vauvengras'. I am confident of the author, less so of the exact maxim number, so I have not cited one.
results.suggested_reattribution: Luc de Clapiers, marquis de Vauvenargues (author name is misspelled in the record)

results.notes: Consistently credited to the playwright Marsha Norman with no competing claimants, and it circulated widely after appearing in magazine quote features in the 1990s. I cannot name the interview, play, or essay it came from, so the citation stays null. Author likely right, source unlocated.

Attributed to Marsha Sinetar, whose subject matter (right livelihood, mind-body integration, contemplative practice) fits the content well - most likely from one of her books such as Do What You Love, the Money Will Follow (1987) or Ordinary People as Monks and Mystics (1986), but I cannot confirm which and will not guess a title.

Attributed to Marsha Sinetar in quote collections; the water-and-obstacle imagery reads like her commentary on an I Ching hexagram, which is consistent with her writing, but I cannot place the book or page. The ellipsis in the text indicates it is already an excerpt from a longer passage, which makes verification harder rather than easier.

results.earliest_print_source: Nonviolent Communication: A Language of Life, Marshall B. Rosenberg, PuddleDancer Press, 1999 (2nd ed. 2003)
results.notes: Genuine Rosenberg, from the opening chapter of Nonviolent Communication, where he introduces observation/feeling/need as the alternative to diagnosis and judgment. Wording and vocabulary match the book directly. Confident in book and author; I have not pinned an exact page.

Widely and consistently credited to McLuhan, but I know of no primary citation - no book, lecture, or interview I can point to. Complicating it: 'Spaceship Earth' is Buckminster Fuller's frame (Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth, 1969), and the line is sometimes handed to Fuller instead. McLuhan is the more common attribution and is plausible, but the evidence I have is secondary repetition, not a source.

Genuine-sounding Graham and consistently attributed to her, from her writing on modern dance in the 1930s-50s. Note a probable transcription corruption: the standard wording is 'We look FOR the dance to impart the sensation of living in an affirmation of life,' not 'look at the dance.' I cannot name the essay or collection with confidence, so no citation.

results.earliest_print_source: Martha: The Life and Work of Martha Graham, Agnes de Mille, Random House, 1991
results.notes: The famous 'keep the channel open' passage, spoken by Graham to Agnes de Mille and recorded by de Mille in her Graham biography. Important caveat for the corpus: this is de Mille's written recollection of Graham's spoken words, not text Graham published, and the widely circulated version has drifted slightly from de Mille's page. Also note the typo carried in this record: 'this expression in unique' should read 'is unique'.

A variant rendering of the same de Mille conversation behind q_0999 ('because there is only one of you in all time'). It circulates as a standalone Graham line, but I cannot match it word for word to de Mille's text, so it may be a paraphrase in transmission rather than a distinct utterance. Author right, exact wording unverified.

Martia Nelson is a real author whose best-known book is 'Coming Home: The Return to True Self' (New World Library, 1993), and this line's vocabulary ('true self', 'expanded nature') is consistent with that book's subject. I cannot confirm from training knowledge that this exact sentence appears there, and I have no independent citation for it. Attribution is plausible but unverified.

Consistently attributed across design literature and talks to Martin LeBlanc, founder of Iconfinder; it circulated widely from around 2013 as a LeBlanc line and I am not aware of any competing attribution. The underlying joke formula ('if you have to explain it, it isn't good') is much older, so LeBlanc's contribution is the UI application rather than the structure. No primary source (original tweet, post, or talk) that I can cite from memory, so this stays below the verified bar.

results.earliest_print_source: "Suffering and Faith," Martin Luther King Jr., The Christian Century, 27 April 1960
results.notes: This is from King's short essay 'Suffering and Faith,' published in The Christian Century on 27 April 1960 (vol. 77, p. 510), written after the Montgomery years. The wording here matches the published text closely; the original reads 'two ways that I could respond to my situation' and uses a colon rather than a dash, so the corpus text is a very light punctuation/wording variant of a genuine passage.

results.earliest_print_source: "The Drum Major Instinct," sermon at Ebenezer Baptist Church, Martin Luther King Jr., 4 February 1968
results.notes: From the closing movement of King's 'Drum Major Instinct' sermon, delivered at Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta on 4 February 1968, two months before his assassination. The passage — 'Everybody can be great, because everybody can serve... You only need a heart full of grace, a soul generated by love' — is well documented in the King Papers and in recordings of the sermon. The corpus rendering ('anybody can serve') is a common variant of the delivered line; the substance and sourcing are solid.

The sentiment is very characteristic of Minsky, who repeatedly argued that scientific commitment must stay revisable and criticized belief held past the evidence. I have a weak recollection of this specific phrasing circulating as a Minsky line from an interview or a talk, but I cannot place a book, article, or date, and I will not guess at one. Plausible but unsourced.

results.earliest_print_source: Courage Doesn't Always Roar, Mary Anne Radmacher, Conari Press, 2009
results.notes: Genuinely Mary Anne Radmacher's. She is a living writer and artist who has publicly claimed and defended this line, which she composed well before the 2009 Conari Press book that takes its title from it (the phrase circulated on her prints and cards from the late 1980s onward). It is frequently misattributed on the internet to Mary Anne Radmacher-Hershey, to 'anonymous', and occasionally to Maya Angelou — all of which resolve back to Radmacher. The book above is the clearest print anchor I can cite, though it postdates the line's origin.

Consistently attributed to Mary Kay Ash in business and motivational quote collections, and consistent in tone with her writing in 'Mary Kay on People Management' (1984) and her autobiography. I cannot locate the sentence in a specific book, speech, or company publication from training knowledge, and much of the Mary Kay Ash quote canon circulates through corporate motivational material without sourcing.

Widely and consistently attributed to Mary Lou Cook, the Santa Fe calligrapher, peace activist, and volunteer-movement figure. The attribution is stable — I know of no competing claimant — but I can point to no book, article, or interview containing it; it appears to have entered circulation through quote anthologies and greeting-card style collections. Stable attribution, absent source.

Attributed with reasonable consistency to Mary Manin Morrissey, the New Thought minister and author of 'Building Your Field of Dreams' (1996) and 'No Less Than Greatness' (2001). The 'one foot on the brakes' image and the letting-go framing match her teaching. I cannot confirm which book, sermon, or newsletter it comes from, and much of her circulating quote material originates in unarchived talks and columns.

Reads as authentic Morrissey — New Thought vocabulary, 'God is our Source' capitalized in the movement's convention — and is attributed to her wherever it appears. But this looks like material from a devotional column, newsletter, or Thanksgiving-season message rather than a book, and I cannot identify the original venue. No source, honest uncertainty.

results.earliest_print_source: "When Death Comes," in New and Selected Poems, Mary Oliver, Beacon Press, 1992
results.notes: This is the closing passage of Mary Oliver's poem 'When Death Comes,' collected in New and Selected Poems (Beacon Press, 1992), which won the National Book Award. The corpus text is accurate but has been flattened from verse into prose — the original is lineated, and the stanza breaks fall after 'into my arms' and after 'full of argument.' Content and attribution are certain; the presentation is a prose rendering of a poem.

Long attributed to Mary Pickford and consistent with the inspirational writing she published in the 1930s, notably 'Why Not Try God?' (1934) and 'My Rendezvous with Life' (1935), which are full of exactly this kind of counsel about failure and second chances. The second sentence ('failure is not the falling down but the staying down') also circulates as an anonymous proverb, which raises the possibility that Pickford was repeating a current saying rather than coining it. I cannot confirm the book or page.

results.earliest_print_source: A Vindication of the Rights of Men, Mary Wollstonecraft, 1790
results.notes: Genuine Wollstonecraft, from 'A Vindication of the Rights of Men' (1790), her reply to Burke. Important caveat: the corpus text has been silently modernized and de-gendered. The original reads, in substance, 'No man chooses evil because it is evil; he only mistakes it for happiness, the good he seeks' — the corpus version rewrites 'no man/he' as 'no one/we' and drops the closing clause 'the good he seeks.' The underlying attribution is verified; the wording as stored is an edited paraphrase and should ideally be restored to the original or marked as adapted.

This line saturates photography quote lists attributed to a bare 'Matt Hardy' with no identifying detail, no publication, and no date. I cannot establish who this Matt Hardy is — the name is shared by a well-known professional wrestler, who is almost certainly not the source, and by several photographers. No traceable origin; the attribution is a name floating free of a person. Treat as effectively anonymous.

Commonly attributed to Max Lucado, the Christian author, and the aphoristic construction fits his style. The same line also circulates in conflict-resolution and mediation training material with no attribution at all, and occasionally credited to others, which suggests it may be a stock saying that attached to Lucado's name rather than a line he coined. I cannot place it in any of his books.

results.earliest_print_source: "Das Wesen der Materie" (The Nature of Matter), lecture in Florence, Max Planck, 1944
results.notes: Genuine Planck, from his 1944 Florence lecture 'Das Wesen der Materie'; the German original runs 'Es gibt keine Materie an sich... Wir müssen hinter dieser Kraft die Existenz eines bewußten intelligenten Geistes annehmen. Dieser Geist ist der Urgrund aller Materie,' preserved in the Archiv zur Geschichte der Max-Planck-Gesellschaft. Caveat worth carrying: this is one of the most heavily context-stripped quotations in physics. It is routinely deployed as evidence that Planck endorsed a personal God or a consciousness-creates-reality metaphysics; his own religious views were considerably more reserved, and 'Geist' here does not map cleanly onto the popular English reading of 'Mind.' Attribution verified, interpretation frequently abused.

Attributed to Maxwell Maltz, the plastic surgeon who wrote 'Psycho-Cybernetics' (1960); the self-image thesis and the link between self-acceptance and perceived opportunity are core Maltz themes, so the attribution is coherent. I cannot confirm the sentence appears in Psycho-Cybernetics or his later books, and the large body of 'Maltz quotes' online includes material from later ghostwritten and revised editions.

Widely circulated as Maxwell Maltz and thematically consistent with Psycho-Cybernetics' argument about self-image and self-worth. No specific book, chapter, or date that I can confirm; this is one of the short aphorisms that spread through motivational compilations detached from any source text.

Genuinely Angelou's in voice and theme, and consistently cited to 'All God's Children Need Traveling Shoes' (1986), the memoir of her years in Ghana, whose central subject is exactly this longing for home. The better-known companion line from that book — 'The ache for home lives in all of us' — is firmly sourced there. I believe this sentence is from the same work but cannot confirm the passage, so I am leaving the print source field empty rather than asserting a citation I have not confirmed.

Attributed to Maya Angelou consistently and without competing claimants; it comes from her spoken remarks — interviews and public conversations in her later years, where she returned often to the theme that empathy is common and the courage to act on it is not. Spoken origin means no clean print citation; I cannot name the specific interview or date.

This is a social-media staple attributed to Angelou and it should be treated with suspicion. I cannot place it in any of her memoirs, poetry, essay collections, or documented interviews, and its register — short, motivational-poster cadence — is unlike her usual construction. Angelou is a strong misattribution magnet: lines by Mary Anne Radmacher, Rumi translators, and anonymous inspirational writers are routinely assigned to her, and 'Still I Rise' fame pulls unattributed uplift toward her name. I have no evidence of a true author, so I am not proposing a reattribution, but the attribution should not be treated as sound.

Angelou used this electricity analogy for talent in interviews, typically extending it — talent, like electricity, is not understood but used, and it makes no judgment about who uses it. The attribution is consistent and the extended form's survival in the record argues for authenticity rather than a manufactured aphorism. I recall it from an interview context but cannot identify the publication or year, so no citation.

Consistently attributed to Angelou and usually cited to 'Wouldn't Take Nothing for My Journey Now' (1993), her collection of short essays, which contains a piece on giving and the giver. The sentence structure ('I have found that among its other benefits') matches that book's essayistic voice more than her memoir prose. I cannot confirm the passage, so the print source field is left empty rather than asserted.

Meg Blackburn Losey is a real author ('The Children of Now', 2007; 'Conversations with the Children of Now', 2008), and the line's vocabulary fits her genre. I have no knowledge of this specific sentence in her published work and cannot find any independent trace of it in what I know. Low confidence; the attribution may be correct but rests on nothing I can check.

The thought is authentically Eckhartian — the via negativa, Abgeschiedenheit (detachment), and his insistence that the soul approaches God by emptying rather than acquiring are central to the German sermons. But this exact English sentence is a modern paraphrase, not a translation of an identifiable sermon passage, and it spread largely through twentieth-century popularizers (Blakney's 1941 translation, and later Matthew Fox's Creation Spirituality writings, which loosely render Eckhart for contemporary readers). Eckhart is a heavy paraphrase magnet: much of what circulates under his name is compression of his ideas rather than his words. Faithful to his theology, unverifiable as his wording.

Consistently attributed to Eckhart and consonant with his German sermons on detachment and poverty of spirit; the fuller form usually runs 'As long as I am this or that, or have this or that, I am not all things and I have not all things.' It circulates through 20th-century English translations (Blakney 1941 and later Matthew Fox anthologies), but I cannot name the specific sermon with confidence from training knowledge, so I am leaving the print source null rather than guessing a sermon number.

The thought is unmistakably Eckhart's central Christmas-sermon theme — the eternal birth of the Word in the soul, and his repeated challenge 'what good is it to me that this birth is always happening, if it does not happen in me?' The wording here reads as a modern loose rendering (of the sort found in devotional anthologies such as Matthew Fox's Meditations with Meister Eckhart) rather than a scholarly translation. Authentic in substance, uncertain as an exact quotation, so I am holding it below the promotion bar.

results.earliest_print_source: Prologus generalis in Opus tripartitum (Opus Propositionum), Meister Eckhart, c. 1305-1311
results.notes: 'Esse est Deus' is the first proposition of the general prologue to Eckhart's unfinished Opus tripartitum, one of the best-documented lines in his Latin corpus and a standard reference point in Eckhart scholarship (McGinn and others discuss it at length). Confidence is 0.85 rather than higher only because the English three-word form is a translation of the Latin proposition, not an independently attested sentence.

results.earliest_print_source: The Language of Letting Go, Melody Beattie, 1990
results.notes: Genuinely Beattie's, from her codependency-recovery daily-meditation writing; the attribution is consistent everywhere it appears and the voice matches her published work. The book citation is the one given in most reputable secondary sources, but I cannot confirm the page or rule out an earlier appearance in Beyond Codependency (1989), so treat the title as probable rather than confirmed. Note that q_1030 is a verbatim duplicate of this entry and should be deduplicated upstream.

results.earliest_print_source: The Language of Letting Go, Melody Beattie, 1990
results.notes: Verbatim duplicate of q_1029 — same verdict. Genuinely Beattie's; the book citation is the standard one but unconfirmed at page level, and an earlier appearance in Beyond Codependency (1989) cannot be excluded. Recommend deduplicating against q_1029.

The author's name is almost certainly Meredith L. Young-Sowers (Agartha, Angelic Messenger Cards, Spiritual Crisis), not 'Young-Sower' — worth correcting in the corpus. I have no independent knowledge of this passage in her published work; it circulates on gratitude and healing quote sites without a source. Honest answer is that I cannot place it.

Uniformly attributed to Michael Altshuler, an American motivational speaker, and I know of no competing claimant — but the attribution rests entirely on quote aggregators and graduation-speech roundups, not on a book, talk transcript, or dated first appearance I can point to. Plausible but unsourced.

Confidence reflects the strength of the Gerber attribution, which is weak. This is a floating proverb that long predates Michael Gerber; it is the popular paraphrase of the Cheshire Cat exchange in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865) — 'if you don't much care where you want to get to, then it doesn't matter which way you go' — and also circulates in Yogi Berra's form ('you'll end up someplace else'). Gerber may well have used it in E-Myth-era writing, but quoting is not coining. No original-author claim should be recorded for him.
results.suggested_reattribution: Popular paraphrase of Lewis Carroll's Cheshire Cat passage, Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865); not original to Michael Gerber

results.earliest_print_source: Lucky Man: A Memoir, Michael J. Fox, 2002
results.notes: This is one of Fox's signature lines and matches the register of his Parkinson's-era memoir; my recollection places it in Lucky Man (2002), which is also the citation given in most secondary sources. I cannot confirm the page, and Fox has repeated the line in interviews, so the memoir may be a repetition rather than the first appearance. Strong on authorship, softer on the exact source.

The name is misspelled — the author credited is Michael LeBoeuf (Working Smart; The Greatest Management Principle in the World; How to Win Customers and Keep Them for Life). The passage is consistently attributed to him on quote sites but I cannot place it in any of his books, and the text as given is garbled ('what you attract with your thoughts think, act and talk negatively'), which is a common signature of aggregator-copied material. Unsourced.

Michael Levy is a contemporary inspirational poet and author (Point of Life), and the style here matches that body of work, so the attribution is plausible. But I have no knowledge of the specific book or poem it comes from, and a living aggregator-circulated author of this kind is exactly the case where I should not manufacture a citation.

results.earliest_print_source: The Neurotic's Notebook, Mignon McLaughlin, 1963
results.notes: A characteristic McLaughlin epigram and well documented as hers; her Wikiquote page is built largely from the two Notebook volumes. The one residual uncertainty is which volume — The Neurotic's Notebook (1963) or The Second Neurotic's Notebook (1966) — so the year should be checked against a print copy before the citation is treated as final.

results.earliest_print_source: The Neurotic's Notebook, Mignon McLaughlin, 1963
results.notes: McLaughlin's single most-quoted aphorism, securely hers and reliably sourced to The Neurotic's Notebook (1963) in Wikiquote and in aphorism anthologies. Occasionally seen floating without attribution or wrongly credited to Germaine Greer, but the McLaughlin attribution is the well-evidenced one.

Consistently and traditionally ascribed to Milarepa (11th-century Tibetan yogi), and entirely in keeping with the counsel in the Mila Grubum (The Hundred Thousand Songs of Milarepa). But I cannot identify which song or which translation this English wording comes from, and Tibetan devotional sayings are heavily paraphrased in circulation. Plausible attribution, unlocated text.

results.earliest_print_source: The Wisdom of the Heart ('Reflections on Writing'), Henry Miller, 1941
results.notes: The bare author field 'Miller' should be expanded to Henry Miller. I recognize this passage from his essay 'Reflections on Writing,' collected in The Wisdom of the Heart (New Directions, 1941), and the argument — art as a means to the life more abundant, defeating itself when made an end — is a recurring Miller theme in that essay. Confident on authorship; the essay/volume citation is from recall rather than a checked page.

results.earliest_print_source: Tropic of Cancer, Henry Miller, 1934
results.notes: Confidence refers to the recorded attribution to 'Milton,' which appears to be a parsing error rather than a real claim about John Milton. The line is Henry Miller's, from the celebrated passage in Tropic of Cancer (1934): 'I love everything that flows...' — and Miller's own sentence contains the phrase 'said the great blind Milton of our times,' his epithet for James Joyce. Almost certainly the corpus captured the word 'Milton' out of that clause. Note this sits adjacent to q_1040, also a Miller entry with a truncated author field, which supports the parsing-error reading.

Thematically very Glaser — the art/design relationship was a lifelong preoccupation of his, running through Art Is Work (2000) and his lectures and essays — but I cannot match this exact sentence to any of his published writing or talks. The formulation 'independent coordinates' is distinctive enough that I would expect to recall it if it were a well-known Glaser line. Plausible, unverified.

This is the famous Sufi maxim 'man arafa nafsahu faqad arafa rabbahu' — 'he who knows himself knows his Lord' — widely quoted in Sufi literature (Ibn Arabi among many others) and often presented as a hadith. Classical hadith scholars rejected it: it appears in none of the canonical collections, and al-Nawawi, Ibn Taymiyya and al-Zarkashi among others judged it not established as a saying of the Prophet. It is sometimes ascribed instead to the early Sufi Yahya ibn Mu'adh al-Razi. Attributing it flatly to Muhammad is not defensible.
results.suggested_reattribution: Sufi maxim of uncertain origin, sometimes ascribed to Yahya ibn Mu'adh al-Razi; not a canonical hadith

results.notes: The name should be Muhammad Ali. Ali did use this line and it appears on materials associated with him, but he did not originate it — 'service is the rent you pay for your room on this earth' is an older circulating aphorism with earlier claimants including Shirley Chisholm and Marian Wright Edelman ('service is the rent we pay for living'), and earlier still it has been credited to the missionary physician Wilfred Grenfell. I do not know the true earliest instance well enough to name one, so I am leaving the reattribution null and flagging Ali as popularizer rather than author.

Almost certainly not Gandhi. The register is late-20th-century American self-help — the escalating 'never / never / never' construction and especially the closing promise 'and your success is guaranteed' are wholly foreign to Gandhi, who framed ahimsa as a discipline and a truth-practice, not as a technique with a guaranteed payoff. I know of no passage resembling this in the Collected Works or in his letters and speeches. Gandhi is one of the strongest misattribution magnets in the corpus, and this has the hallmarks of a seminar handout attributed to him for authority. No true origin identifiable, so no reattribution offered.

results.earliest_print_source: The Matrix (screenplay/film), written and directed by Lana and Lilly Wachowski, Warner Bros., 1999
results.notes: A genuine and famous line of Morpheus's dialogue from The Matrix (1999), spoken to Neo in the construct/chair scene. Source is confirmed and dated. One caveat for the corpus: 'Morpheus' is a fictional character, not an author — if the corpus distinguishes speaker from author, the writing credit belongs to the Wachowskis and the character should be recorded as the speaker.
results.suggested_reattribution: Lana and Lilly Wachowski (writers); Morpheus is the fictional speaker

results.earliest_print_source: The Shoes of the Fisherman, Morris L. West, 1963
results.notes: I recognize this as West's, and my recollection places it in The Shoes of the Fisherman (1963), where it belongs to a longer reflective passage that continues into a statement about accepting every consequence of living and dying. The attribution to West is consistent wherever the line appears. Holding at 0.7 because I am working from recall of the novel rather than a checked page, and West reused similar material across his fiction and essays.

Consistently attributed to Mother Teresa and fully in keeping with how she spoke about the Missionaries of Charity's work — joy as the surprising thing, not the labor. But I cannot locate it in a specific address, interview, or book; it circulates through devotional collections and secondhand quotation. Plausible and in-voice, but unsourced, so it stays below the promotion bar.

results.earliest_print_source: The Silent Revolution: Dynamic Leadership in the Student Council, Kent M. Keith, 1968
results.notes: This is one of the best-documented misattributions in circulation. The text is an adapted version of 'The Paradoxical Commandments,' written by Kent M. Keith in 1968 while he was a Harvard undergraduate, published in his booklet The Silent Revolution: Dynamic Leadership in the Student Council. A shortened version titled 'Anyway' was posted on the wall of Mother Teresa's children's home in Calcutta, which is how her name became attached; it was later reprinted in books about her, cementing the error. The closing 'it is between you and God' line is part of that Calcutta adaptation. Keith's authorship is well established and he has written about it publicly.

The idiom is authentically hers — 'Jesus in his distressing disguise' was a formula Mother Teresa used repeatedly about the poor and the dying, and the sentence structure matches her spoken English. I cannot, however, tie this exact sentence to a dated address, interview, or book, and the wording varies across versions. Note also that the corpus text carries dated and dehumanizing phrasing ('the cripple, the mental') that may be a transcription of her idiom or an aggregator's corruption; worth a human editorial decision independent of the provenance question.

Circulates most often as 'God has not called me to be successful; He has called me to be faithful,' consistently ascribed to Mother Teresa in devotional literature and quote collections. I cannot place it in any of her published writings, letters, or recorded addresses, and the wording varies noticeably between sources, which is a common signature of an oral/secondhand attribution. Plausible but unverified.

Agrees with the input flag. Extremely widely attributed to Mother Teresa and consistent with her recorded themes, but I know of no primary source — no speech, interview, or book of hers that I can place it in. It spread heavily through greeting-card and internet quote compilations. Honest answer: attribution is plausible and uncontested, evidence is absent.

A genuine and consistently attributed Mother Teresa saying, though this is one of several circulating wordings. Better-known variants: 'I know that the work is only a drop in the ocean, but if the drop were not there, the ocean would be missing something,' and 'We ourselves feel that what we are doing is just a drop in the ocean. But the ocean would be less because of that missing drop.' Attribution is strong and uniform across sources; the specific phrasing here I cannot tie to a primary text, so I am holding below the 0.80 promotion bar.

One of the most durable and consistently attributed Mother Teresa lines; standard wording is 'We can do no great things, only small things with great love.' Attribution is uniform across decades of sources and she is recorded using the formulation in talks. The corpus entry has two hygiene problems: the author is misspelled 'Mother Theresa,' and the text is a garbled variant ('We can not do great things, just small things...') with inconsistent capitalization of 'Love.' I could not place the exact primary utterance, so this stays at strong-secondary rather than verified.

'Mu Mon-kwan' is not a person — it is a garbling of Mumonkan (無門關), the Japanese title of The Gateless Gate, the 1228 koan collection compiled by the Chinese Chan master Wumen Huikai (Japanese: Mumon Ekai). The underlying saying is Wumen's verse commentary, familiar in English from Paul Reps' Zen Flesh, Zen Bones as roughly: 'It is too clear and so it is hard to see. A dunce once searched for fire with a lighted lantern. Had he known what fire was, he could have cooked his rice much sooner.' The text here is a loose modern paraphrase, not any translation I recognize, so I am not citing the Mumonkan as the print source for this wording. The idea is authentically Wumen's; the sentence is not.
results.suggested_reattribution: Wumen Huikai (Mumon Ekai), The Gateless Gate / Mumonkan, c. 1228 — as a paraphrase, not a quotation

results.notes: Consistently attributed to Muhammad Ali and stylistically plausible for him, but I cannot place it in a specific interview, press conference, or in The Greatest: My Own Story (1975). Ali is a moderate misattribution magnet — motivational copy written for and about him is routinely recirculated as his own words (see q_1057). Attribution here is uncontested but unsourced.

This is advertising copy, not Ali. The passage is the manifesto text of the adidas 'Impossible Is Nothing' campaign launched in 2004, developed by the agency 180/TBWA, whose flagship spots featured Muhammad Ali (and archival footage of him alongside his daughter Laila). The final line 'Impossible is nothing' is the campaign tagline, which is the strongest tell. Ali's name and image were licensed to the campaign; the words were written for it. Widely recirculated as an Ali quotation ever since, including in books and on quote sites. I am confident the campaign is the origin and correspondingly low-confidence in the Ali attribution.

results.earliest_print_source: Everyday Blessings: The Inner Work of Mindful Parenting, Myla and Jon Kabat-Zinn, 1997
results.notes: The joint byline points to Everyday Blessings (Hyperion, 1997), which is Myla and Jon Kabat-Zinn's only co-authored book, so the source attribution is near-certain even though I cannot confirm the sentences verbatim against the text. The definition also closely tracks Jon Kabat-Zinn's standard formulation ('paying attention in a particular way: on purpose, in the present moment, and non-judgmentally,' Full Catastrophe Living, 1990 / Wherever You Go, There You Are, 1994), which is consistent with a co-authored restatement rather than a fabrication. Holding below 0.80 because the wording is unverified.

Attributed to Myla Kabat-Zinn, most likely drawn from Everyday Blessings (1997), the book she co-wrote with Jon Kabat-Zinn, where she writes in her own voice in places. I cannot confirm the line appears there or anywhere else I can name. Myla Kabat-Zinn has a thin independent publication record, which makes the quote hard to source and easy to misassign between the two authors. Honest verdict: unverified.

The canonical form of this saying is Buddhist scripture, not Nagarjuna: Dhammapada 204, 'santuṭṭhī paramaṃ dhanaṃ' — 'contentment is the greatest wealth.' Nagarjuna does echo it in the Suhṛllekha (Letter to a Friend), where he cites the Buddha to the effect that contentment is the supreme form of wealth, so the ascription is not baseless — but it makes Nagarjuna a transmitter rather than the author, and this four-word English form matches the Dhammapada rendering, not a specific Suhṛllekha translation I can name. Attribution as it stands is weak.
results.suggested_reattribution: Dhammapada 204 (attributed to the Buddha); Nagarjuna restates it in the Suhṛllekha, quoting the Buddha

results.notes: Naoto Fukasawa is a real and well-documented Japanese industrial designer (MUJI, ±0, Naoto Fukasawa Design), and the sentiment matches his stated 'without thought' philosophy of design as embedded in everyday behavior and environment. The line circulates in design-quote collections, most plausibly extracted from an interview or from his Phaidon monograph (2007). I cannot place it in a specific text or interview, and designer quotes of this kind are frequently paraphrased in circulation.

results.earliest_print_source: Think and Grow Rich, Napoleon Hill, 1937
results.notes: Genuinely Hill's, and one of the load-bearing lines of Think and Grow Rich (1937), where the canonical wording is 'Every adversity, every failure, every heartache carries with it the seed of an equal or greater benefit.' Hill repeated variants across his later work and lectures. The corpus text is a compressed variant ('Every adversity or failure... an equivalent or a greater benefit'), so the attribution is solid while the exact phrasing is non-canonical — consider normalizing to the 1937 wording.

The joint byline points to Success Through a Positive Mental Attitude (1960), the only book Napoleon Hill and W. Clement Stone wrote together, and the passage's content — quiet reflection, warning against confusing motion with effectiveness — fits that book's register. I cannot confirm the wording appears there, and I have no independent recollection of this passage, so I am not asserting the citation. Attribution to the pair is plausible on structural grounds only.

Natalie Goldberg is the author of Writing Down the Bones (1986) and Wild Mind (1990), and this is entirely consistent with her teaching on slowness, composting, and present-moment creativity. The conversational register ('For me, slowing down has been...') reads like an interview or magazine Q&A rather than her published prose. I cannot place the specific interview or book, so the attribution stands as plausible-but-unsourced.

Nathaniel Alexander Owings (1903-1984) was a real architect, co-founder of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, and author of The American Aesthetic (1969) and the memoir The Spaces in Between: An Architect's Journey (1973); the environmental-humanist tone fits The American Aesthetic in particular. But I have no recollection of this passage in either book or in any secondary citation, and a quote this obscure with no accompanying source is hard to distinguish from a misattribution. Low confidence, no citation offered.

Consistent with Nathaniel Branden's body of work on self-esteem and self-honoring — most likely from Honoring the Self (1983) or The Six Pillars of Self-Esteem (1994) — but 'nurture the soul' is a slightly atypical register for Branden, who generally wrote in secular psychological language. I cannot place the passage in a specific book, and cannot rule out that it comes from a self-help anthology quoting him loosely.

This is a recognizable Branden formulation and is attributed to him with unusual consistency; 'the practice of self-acceptance' is one of the six pillars in The Six Pillars of Self-Esteem (1994), and the refusal-to-be-adversarial framing is how he defines it there. I believe the book is the source but cannot confirm the sentence verbatim, so I am naming it in these notes rather than asserting it as a citation, and holding below the 0.80 promotion bar.

Two problems. First, data hygiene: the stored text includes its own framing ('Nathaniel Hawthorne once famously said, ...') plus curly quotes — the quotation itself should be extracted and the frame dropped. Second, provenance: the documented Hawthorne passage on this theme is from his American Note-Books and runs, in substance, 'Happiness in this world, when it comes, comes incidentally. Make it the object of pursuit, and it leads us a wild-goose chase... Follow some other object, and very possibly we may find that we have caught happiness without dreaming of it.' The butterfly simile is the popular, much-later circulating form, and I cannot confirm Hawthorne wrote the butterfly wording himself. It may be a paraphrase that hardened into a quotation. Attribution to Hawthorne for the idea is sound; for these words, unverified.

No credible traditional source. 'Navajo saying' is a generic ascription of exactly the kind that inspirational literature invents, and the language here is modern therapeutic English — 'challenge us to grow,' 'move beyond the knowable,' 'elemental and essential nature' — not translated Diné oral tradition. 'Big medicine teachers' reads as a settler-inflected pastiche of Native idiom. Pseudo-Native-American attributions are a well-documented category of fabrication (cf. the Chief Seattle speech). I know of no Navajo prayer, ceremonial text, or ethnographic record containing this. Recommend rejecting or relabeling as anonymous modern.

Attributed to Neale Donald Walsch with strong consistency across sources, and he has used and endorsed it himself, which distinguishes it from the usual orphan aphorism. The sentiment appears in the Conversations with God material ('Life begins at the end of your comfort zone' is often traced to that body of work), but I cannot pin it to a specific book or page. Note this is one of the most heavily recirculated single-sentence quotes on the internet, which tends to detach lines from their sources.

results.earliest_print_source: Conversations with God: An Uncommon Dialogue, Book 1, Neale Donald Walsch, 1995
results.notes: 'What would love do now?' is a signature question of the Conversations with God material and is closely identified with Book 1 (1995); the surrounding cadence here — 'Yea, let all those who have ears to hear' — matches the book's deliberately scriptural voice. I am confident about the work; I cannot confirm this exact passage or its page, so the citation is at book level and the score stays below the promotion bar.

results.earliest_print_source: Under Whose Shade: A Story of a Pioneer in the Swan River Valley of Manitoba, Wes Henderson, 1986
results.notes: This one has a real and unusually well-traced provenance for a folk-sounding aphorism: it is reported as the advice of Nelson Henderson, a Manitoba farmer, recorded by his son Wes Henderson in the family memoir Under Whose Shade (1986) — the book's title comes from the saying. The frequently seen preface is 'The true meaning of life is to plant trees under whose shade you do not expect to sit.' I am confident in the Henderson origin and reasonably confident in the book; note the broader tree-planting sentiment is ancient (cf. the Greek proverb about old men planting trees) and Nelson Henderson is the reporter of this phrasing, not the inventor of the idea.

Ubiquitously attributed to Nelson Mandela and quoted as his during his lifetime without evident objection, which is meaningful evidence — but I cannot place it in any speech, letter, or book of his, and the attribution appears to become common only around the 2000s. It also circulated widely through advertising and campaign copy, a route that manufactures false attributions. Mandela is a moderate misattribution magnet. Plausible, unsourced; treat as attributed-unverified until a primary text is found. NOTE: this quote is duplicated in this batch as q_1075 — deduplicate.

This is Mandela's well-documented 'lead from the front / lead from the back' teaching, which reached wide circulation through Richard Stengel — his TIME cover story 'Mandela: His 8 Lessons of Leadership' (July 2008) and his book Mandela's Way (2010), both drawing on years of recorded conversations while ghostwriting Long Walk to Freedom. Stengel is a credible firsthand channel, so this sits well above the usual orphan-quote baseline. I cannot confirm the exact wording against either text, so I am naming the likely channel here rather than asserting a citation.

Exact duplicate of q_1073 within this batch — same text, same author. Verdict is identical: ubiquitously attributed to Nelson Mandela and quoted as his during his lifetime, but I cannot place it in any speech, letter, or book, and it spread heavily through advertising and campaign copy. Plausible, unsourced. Recommend merging with q_1073 at the dedupe stage.

Consistently attributed to Nicholas Evans and, in most citations, to his 1995 novel The Horse Whisperer, where it reads as Tom Booker's voice. I recall the passage as belonging to that novel but cannot confirm chapter or exact wording from memory, and a similar sentiment appears in the 1998 film adaptation, so I am leaving the print source blank rather than asserting a page. Author attribution is plausible and uncontested; the work-level citation is not confirmed.

Widely circulated as Bohr but I cannot place it in any Bohr paper, lecture, or documented conversation. Bohr's genuinely sourced remark in this family is the 'crazy enough' exchange reported second-hand by Freeman Dyson (recounting a 1958 Columbia seminar on Heisenberg and Pauli's unified field theory): 'we are all agreed that your theory is crazy... whether it is crazy enough to have a chance of being correct.' The wording here reads like a later prose expansion of that idea, possibly from a management or innovation anthology rather than Bohr himself. No primary source; attribution unconfirmed.

results.earliest_print_source: Also sprach Zarathustra (Thus Spoke Zarathustra), Friedrich Nietzsche, 1883-1885 - Part IV, 'On the Higher Man', §20
results.notes: Genuine Nietzsche. German original: 'Und verloren sei uns der Tag, wo nicht Ein Mal getanzt wurde! Und falsch heisse uns jede Wahrheit, bei der es nicht Ein Gelaechter gab!' The English here is a common paraphrastic rendering ('we should consider every day lost...') rather than a literal translation of the imperative, but the source is not in doubt.

Universally attributed to Nietzsche and stylistically consistent with the flight imagery of Zarathustra, but I cannot locate it in a specific work from memory. My recollection is that this line sits in the unsourced or disputed section of Nietzsche quotation compilations rather than being traced to a published aphorism. Plausible but unconfirmed; I am not inventing a locus.

Corresponds to a German aphorism I associate with Nietzsche's middle period - roughly 'Der Glaube an die Wahrheit beginnt mit dem Zweifel an allen bisher geglaubten Wahrheiten' - most often cited to Human, All Too Human, Volume II (Assorted Opinions and Maxims). I am confident enough in the authorship to call it plausible but not confident enough in the volume or aphorism number to print a citation. Author likely correct; source unverified.

results.earliest_print_source: Jenseits von Gut und Boese (Beyond Good and Evil), Friedrich Nietzsche, 1886 - §80
results.notes: Beyond Good and Evil aphorism 80 opens 'Was erklaert worden ist, das geht uns Nichts mehr an' - most commonly rendered 'A thing that is explained ceases to concern us.' The corpus wording ('Anything that has been explained ceases to interest us') is a variant translation of the same line, not a separate quotation. Source is secure; only the English rendering differs.

Attributed to Nietzsche in quotation collections. The epigrammatic form is consistent with Human, All Too Human or the Nachlass, but I cannot place it in any specific text and I have no recollection of a German original for it, which weakens my confidence that it is Nietzsche at all rather than a translator's or anthologist's line. Unverified.

I cannot place this in Nietzsche's published works or correspondence. The image (singing alone in an empty house) is not one I can match to any passage I know, and the sentence rhythm reads more like a modern inspirational paraphrase than like Nietzsche's aphoristic style in translation. Possibly a loose rendering of a letter, possibly not his at all. No source; honest answer is that I do not know.

Newton's remark on patient thought is genuinely documented, but the best-attested wording is the one recorded in David Brewster's Memoirs of the Life, Writings, and Discoveries of Sir Isaac Newton (1855): 'If I have done the public any service, it is due to patient thought.' The variant here ('any valuable discoveries... patient attention... than to any other talent') circulates widely in 19th and 20th century collections and may derive from a separate reported conversation, but I cannot confirm which. Attribution to Newton is sound in substance; the exact wording is a variant I will not cite to a page.

Consistently attributed to Kazantzakis and thoroughly consistent with his metaphysics of will in The Saviors of God and Report to Greco. Most citations point to Report to Greco (1961, English 1965). I recall the sentiment strongly as his but cannot confirm which book or translation the English wording comes from, so no print source is asserted.

Zorba's line from Zorba the Greek. Note that this exact English phrasing is the one spoken in Michael Cacoyannis's 1964 film adaptation ('A man needs a little madness, or else he never dares cut the rope and be free'), which is where its popularity comes from; the corresponding passage in Kazantzakis's 1946 novel (English translation by Carl Wildman, 1952) carries the same sense in different words. So the sentiment is Kazantzakis's, but the wording may be the screenwriter's. Attributing to the author is defensible; I am not printing a page citation because I cannot distinguish novel wording from screenplay wording.

Attributed to Norman Cousins across many collections and entirely consistent with his nuclear-age advocacy writing (Modern Man Is Obsolete, 1945; Human Options, 1981). I cannot place it in a specific book, essay, or Saturday Review editorial from memory. Author plausible; source unverified.

Reads authentically as Peale - the flat assertion of a 'demonstrable fact' followed by the love/fear inversion is his characteristic register, and the theme runs through The Power of Positive Thinking (1952) and his later devotional writing. But I cannot pin it to a specific book or Guideposts piece, and Peale's corpus is large and heavily anthologized. Attribution plausible, source not established.

O. Wayne Rollins (1912-1991), founder of Rollins Inc., is a low-profile figure whose quoted remarks come almost entirely from business-quotation compilations and company/foundation retrospectives rather than from published writing. I have no independent knowledge of where or when he said this. The sentiment is a commonplace of American business memoir, so the attribution could easily have drifted. Unverified.

Consistent with Og Mandino's late motivational writing, and 'Count your blessings' is one of the numbered rules in A Better Way to Live (1990), his book of seventeen 'Rules to Live By.' I believe this expanded passage is that rule's text, but I cannot confirm the wording or the rule number from memory, so no citation is printed. Author attribution reliable; exact source unconfirmed.

One of the best known lines credited to Og Mandino and stylistically his (the 'I will...' vow construction is the scroll form used throughout The Greatest Salesman in the World, 1968). I cannot confirm whether it comes from that book, from A Better Way to Live, or from one of his lectures, so the source is left blank. Author attribution well established in secondary sources.

Generic self-help maxim of a kind that circulated in New Thought and success literature well before Mandino (close variants appear in Napoleon Hill and Charles Popplestone-era writing). Attributed to Mandino in modern collections but with no traceable source, and the idea is too common for the attribution to be safe. Unverified and possibly drifted.

Same provenance situation as the 'Count your blessings' passage - this is almost certainly one of the seventeen rules in A Better Way to Live (1990), whose entries share exactly this structure (imperative opening, long qualifying clause, short closing command: 'Never take yourself too seriously'). I cannot confirm the rule number or verify the wording, so no citation. Author attribution reliable.

Attributed to the Greek-American poet Olga Broumas in quotation collections, but I cannot locate it in Beginning with O (1977) or her later books, and it does not read like her line-broken, Sappho-inflected verse. The sentiment matches a family of older proverbs about roses and thorns (commonly given as Persian or Turkish, e.g. 'he who wants a rose must respect the thorn'), which is the more likely origin. I do not know the true source, so no reattribution is asserted - only doubt about this one.

Goldsmith did write on this theme: in The Citizen of the World (1760-62) he gives 'Our greatest glory consists not in never falling, but in rising every time we fall' - and he presents it there as a Confucian saying, not his own. The wording in this record ('getting up just one more time than you fall') is a modern counting-style rewording that I cannot trace to Goldsmith or to any 18th-century text; it appears in 20th-century motivational literature and is variously credited to Goldsmith and to others. So the attribution is at best inherited from a paraphrase of a paraphrase. Not calling it likely_misattributed only because the idea does descend from Goldsmith's page; the words almost certainly are not his.

results.earliest_print_source: The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table, Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr., 1858
results.notes: Two errors compounded. The original is by Oliver Wendell Holmes SENIOR, the physician-essayist, not his son the Supreme Court justice: 'Every now and then a man's mind is stretched by a new idea or sensation, and never shrinks back to its former dimensions.' The familiar 'One's mind, once stretched by a new idea, never regains its original dimensions' is a 20th-century compression of that sentence, not Holmes's wording. Father/son confusion is the standard failure mode with this quote. Recommend reattributing to Holmes Sr. and, if the corpus wants exactness, restoring the 1858 wording.

results.earliest_print_source: Lady Windermere's Fan, Oscar Wilde, 1892 - Act III
results.notes: Genuine Wilde, from the Act III club scene in Lady Windermere's Fan. The full exchange continues '...The last is much the worst; the last is a real tragedy!' Confident about play and act; slightly less certain which of the Act III dandies (Dumby) speaks the line, but that does not affect authorship. Wilde later reworked the same paradox elsewhere in his prose.

results.earliest_print_source: 'The Critic as Artist', in Intentions, Oscar Wilde, 1891
results.notes: Genuine Wilde, from the Gilbert-Ernest dialogue in The Critic as Artist. Note the wording drift: Wilde's sentence ends 'an unbiased opinion is always absolutely valueless,' not 'always useless.' Recommend restoring 'absolutely valueless' if the corpus wants the authorial text. Source itself is not in doubt.

results.earliest_print_source: Lady Windermere's Fan, Oscar Wilde, 1892 - Act I
results.notes: One of the securest Wilde attributions there is: Lord Darlington's line in Act I of Lady Windermere's Fan, in reply to Lady Windermere's 'You have a great many ideals.' Quoted accurately and complete.

Authentic Wilde in substance and voice; my recollection places it in the critical prose of Intentions (1891), most likely The Critic as Artist, where he returns repeatedly to the public's hostility toward genius and its indulgence of mediocrity. Because I cannot confirm the essay with certainty - it could equally be from The Soul of Man Under Socialism (1891), which treats the same theme - I am not printing a source. Authorship strongly supported; locus unconfirmed.

Circulates in 20th-century quote compilations under Wilde's name, but I cannot place it in any Wilde play, essay, novel, or letter I know. The epigrammatic balance is Wilde-like, which is exactly what makes aphorisms stick to him. No source; treating as unverified rather than assuming the collections are right.

Very widely attributed to Wilde and one of the most-reprinted 'Wilde' lines, but to my knowledge it sits in the unsourced/attributed section of the Wilde record rather than in any of his published works. Consistent attribution, zero primary evidence. (Input text has a typo: 'you enemies' should read 'your enemies'.)

results.earliest_print_source: The Picture of Dorian Gray, Oscar Wilde, 1890/1891
results.notes: Genuine Wilde, spoken by Lord Henry Wotton in Chapter 2. The canonical wording runs '...nothing can cure the soul but the senses, just as nothing can cure the senses but the soul.' The record here reverses the clauses and substitutes 'there is nothing that will cure' — same sentence, loosely requoted. Recommend restoring Wilde's wording.

A well-known false Wilde. It appears nowhere in his works and the Wilde attribution is a late-20th-century development; earlier circulation of the sentiment is anonymous aphorism/greeting-card material. Classic misattribution-magnet behaviour. No credible author is identifiable, so apocryphal rather than likely_misattributed. (Input also misspells 'everone'.)

results.earliest_print_source: The Picture of Dorian Gray, Oscar Wilde, 1890/1891; Lady Windermere's Fan, Oscar Wilde, 1892
results.notes: Both halves are authentically Wilde but they are two separate quotations welded together. 'The only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it' is Lord Henry in Dorian Gray ch. 2; 'I can resist everything except temptation' is Lord Darlington in Lady Windermere's Fan, Act I. The record also corrupts the second line to 'buy temptation'. Recommend splitting into two records and fixing the typo.

Diction, cadence, and subject are strongly consistent with Osho's transcribed discourses, and the line circulates under his name. But his corpus is thousands of transcribed talks compiled into hundreds of volumes, and I cannot name the specific discourse or book. Plausible author, unlocatable source.

The 'masters only show the way, nobody can walk for you' theme is a recurring Osho motif and the phrasing reads as a genuine discourse transcript. I cannot identify which talk or published volume it comes from. Attribution plausible but unsourced.

Widely circulated as Osho and consistent with his teaching on uniqueness, acceptance, and love. I have a vague sense it appears in one of the compiled volumes on love or courage, but I cannot confirm which, and I will not guess a title. Unsourced.

Long associated with P. T. Barnum and often described as his motto; it recurs in circus histories and Barnum memorial contexts. I cannot place it in his autobiography or his published writings, and I do not know the earliest printing. Consistent attribution to a non-magnet figure is mild positive evidence, but not enough for 'attributed'.

This is dialogue written for the fictionalised Barnum in the 2017 film The Greatest Showman, not a saying of the historical showman. The phrasing is modern-motivational and unlike 19th-century Barnum's prose. A large wave of pseudo-Barnum quotes entered circulation after that film. Reattribution is to the film's screenwriters; I am confident about the film origin but will not name individual credits from memory.
results.suggested_reattribution: The Greatest Showman (2017 film) — dialogue written for the P. T. Barnum character

results.notes: One of the most-reprinted 'Picasso' lines, consistently attributed to him across mid-20th-century onward compilations, but I know of no primary source — no interview, letter, or recorded conversation I can point to. Picasso is a moderate misattribution magnet for aphorisms about art. Attribution plausible, evidence weak.

Widely quoted as Picasso in compilations and business/creativity literature; I cannot locate it in Brassaï's or Gilot's recorded conversations or any interview I know. No primary source, and the sentiment is generic enough to have drifted onto him.

The lump-of-sugar image is distinctive and specific rather than generic-inspirational, which argues for a real recorded remark, and my sense is that it comes from one of the memoir-conversation books about Picasso (Gilot or Brassaï). I cannot confirm which, so I am not citing one. Attribution likely correct, source unconfirmed.

Circulates under Picasso's name in creativity anthologies. Possibly a condensation of remarks recorded in the conversation memoirs, but I cannot place it and the flat phrasing reads like a compilation paraphrase rather than a transcribed utterance. Unsourced.

No evidence Picasso ever said this. The attribution was massively amplified by Steve Jobs quoting it in the 1990s/2000s. The documented antecedents belong to the literary-criticism tradition: W. H. Davenport Adams (1892) on poets who 'imitate and improve' versus those who 'steal and spoil', and T. S. Eliot in The Sacred Wood (1920), 'Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal.' Those are ancestors, not the same sentence, so I am not naming a single true author.

There is a real documented root: Herbert Read reported Picasso's remark on seeing an exhibition of children's drawings, roughly 'When I was as old as these children I could draw like Raphael; it took me many years to learn how to draw like these children' (reported in the British press in the mid-1950s). The version here — 'four years to paint like Raphael, but a lifetime to paint like a child' — is a later mutation with no documented basis. Kernel genuine, this wording not. (Input also has a typo: 'I took me'.)

I have no knowledge of Pamela Harper as a quoted author and cannot place this passage. The register — mantra, divine opportunities, prosperity — suggests a contributor piece in a prosperity or affirmation anthology. Nothing traceable in my training knowledge; honest answer is that I do not know.

results.earliest_print_source: The Alchemist (O Alquimista), Paulo Coelho, 1988
results.notes: A genuine line from The Alchemist, part of the book's central 'where your heart is, there your treasure is' motif spoken to Santiago (itself echoing Matthew 6:21). English wording varies slightly by translation/edition. Note the author name is misspelled in the record: 'Paolo Coelho' should be 'Paulo Coelho'.

Consistent with Papaji's (H. W. L. Poonja's) satsang idiom, and his recorded corpus is largely transcribed dialogues compiled by students, which makes any single aphorism hard to source. I cannot place this line in any specific compilation. Low confidence, no source.

Thoroughly characteristic of Yogananda's voice and doctrine ('soul-reflections of the one God', 'One Spirit'), and likely drawn from the Self-Realization Fellowship collections of his talks (Man's Eternal Quest, The Divine Romance, or similar). I cannot confirm which volume, so I am not citing one. Attribution plausible, source unlocated.

This passage does not appear in the Yoga Sutras in any translation I know. The Sutras are terse aphorisms in Sanskrit; this is expansive 20th-century motivational English ('dormant forces, faculties and talents'). It spread widely through Western business-creativity and New Thought literature in the 1980s-90s while carrying a 'Patanjali' label. Not Patanjali; I cannot identify the actual modern author, so no reattribution is offered.

Patricia Monighan Nourot was a scholar of children's play and a co-author in that literature, so the work/play distinction here is topically apt for her. But I cannot place the sentence in any of her publications, and lines like this in play scholarship are often quoted from a child rather than authored by the researcher. Weak evidence.

Consistently attributed to Paul Boese across decades of quote collections, with circulation traceable to 1960s-era newspaper quote columns/fillers. The attribution's stability to an otherwise obscure name is itself decent evidence — misattributions drift toward famous people, not away from them. I do not know the exact original printing, so I am leaving the citation null rather than guessing.

Paul Ferrini is a real author in the Course-in-Miracles-adjacent tradition (Love Without Conditions and related titles), and this passage matches his register closely. I cannot identify the specific book or article. Plausible author, no locatable source.

Strongly consistent with Paul Hawken's thinking on inquiry-driven enterprise, and my impression is that it comes from Growing a Business (1987), whose argument leans on questions over expertise. I am not confident enough to enter that as a citation, so the source field stays null. Attribution likely correct, source unconfirmed.

I cannot identify 'Paul Jewkes' as a documented author, executive, or public figure in my training knowledge, and I cannot place this line in any published source. The underlying image is an old agricultural proverb ('a crooked furrow is better than an unplowed field') that circulates in farming, LDS, and management-advice contexts with no fixed attribution; the named attribution here may be to a private individual or a local speaker. No evidence either way, so no reattribution is offered.

A well-known Paul Rand aphorism, quoted consistently in design literature and in collections of his remarks on logo and identity work, with no competing attribution that I am aware of. I believe it comes from his own writing (most likely 'Design, Form, and Chaos', 1993, or a late interview), but I cannot confirm the specific volume or page from memory, so I am leaving the print source null rather than guessing.

One of the most frequently repeated Paul Rand lines, attributed to him uniformly across design writing, interviews, and obituary coverage. I know of no rival claimant and no reason to doubt it. I cannot name the first printed appearance, so the source field is left null.

results.earliest_print_source: Design, Form, and Chaos, Paul Rand, 1993 (commonly cited; page not confirmed)
results.notes: This passage is distinctly Rand's prose and is quoted at length in design literature, consistently sourced to 'Design, Form, and Chaos' (Yale University Press, 1993). I am confident in the author; I am moderately but not fully confident in the book, and I have not confirmed a page, so the source is recorded as commonly-cited rather than verified. Note that the closing sentence ('To design is to transform prose into poetry') is sometimes quoted separately from the rest.

Very widely and consistently attributed to Paul Tillich, and the sentiment fits his theology of love, justice, and power. However, I cannot place it in a specific sermon, essay, or volume, and the line circulates almost entirely through quote collections rather than through citation to a Tillich text. Plausible but unconfirmed; kept below the promotion bar for that reason.

Attributed consistently to Paulo Coelho and stylistically consistent with his aphoristic writing (possibly from 'Like the Flowing River' or from his blog/social posts, which are a genuine and heavily quoted source for him). I cannot identify the specific book or post, and a large volume of Coelho-attributed material online is unsourced, so I am holding confidence at the moderate level.

results.earliest_print_source: O Alquimista (The Alchemist), Paulo Coelho, 1988
results.notes: This is from 'The Alchemist'. The vocabulary is internal to that novel — 'the Soul of the World' is the book's own term, and the beginner's-luck / severe-testing motif is stated by the alchemist to Santiago near the end of the journey. The final sentence ('the darkest hour of the night comes just before the dawn') also appears in the novel. Quoted here with a minor grammatical slip ('come' for 'comes') relative to the standard English translation.

results.earliest_print_source: O Alquimista (The Alchemist), Paulo Coelho, 1988
results.notes: A well-known line from 'The Alchemist', spoken by Melchizedek, the old king of Salem, early in the novel. Attribution is uncontested and the line is traceable to the text itself rather than only to quote collections.

results.earliest_print_source: Start Where You Are: A Guide to Compassionate Living, Pema Chödrön, 1994 (commonly cited; not confirmed)
results.notes: The gloriousness/wretchedness pairing is a signature Pema Chödrön teaching from her lojong material, and I associate this formulation with 'Start Where You Are' (1994). I am confident about the author and the teaching; I am less certain which of her books this exact sentence appears in — 'The Wisdom of No Escape' covers similar ground — so the source is flagged as unconfirmed.

Consistently attributed to Pema Chödrön and characteristic of her writing on fear; I associate it with 'When Things Fall Apart' (1997), where she treats fear and trembling as a signal rather than an enemy, but I cannot confirm the book or chapter well enough to record it as a citation. Author attribution is solid; the source is not.

Widely and consistently attributed to Pema Chödrön, and squarely within her recurring teaching that difficult people are the practice. I cannot pin it to a specific book ('The Wisdom of No Escape' and 'Start Where You Are' are both plausible), so no print source is recorded.

Attribution to Pema Chödrön is consistent across sources and the passage reads as transcribed teaching in her voice (the bottomless-heart image recurs in her bodhichitta talks). I cannot identify which book or talk it comes from, so the source is left null.

Attributed to Pema Chödrön across quote collections and consistent with her teaching on fixed views and 'the truth we cling to'. I cannot locate a specific source text, and this shorter aphoristic form is the kind most vulnerable to being condensed from a longer passage, so I am holding confidence moderate.

Extremely widely circulated as Pema Chödrön, and she does use the sky-and-weather metaphor for mind and passing states. The caution is that the sky/clouds image is common across Tibetan Buddhist teaching generally (it long predates her), so this compressed slogan form may be a popularized condensation of her wording rather than a verbatim sentence. Author attribution is likely correct; wording and source are unconfirmed.

This is Pema Chödrön quoting someone else. The line originates with Karlfried Graf Dürckheim, the German psychotherapist and Zen teacher — his formulation runs roughly 'Only to the extent that a man exposes himself over and over again to annihilation can that which is indestructible be found in him.' Chödrön quotes it (with attribution to Dürckheim) in her own work, most likely 'When Things Fall Apart', which is how it got detached and re-credited to her. I am confident about Dürckheim as the source author; I cannot name the specific Dürckheim title from memory.

I can find no author named 'Philip Toshido' in my training knowledge — not as a writer, teacher, or public figure — and the name itself looks irregular (Toshido is not a standard surname; this may be a corrupted or invented name). The sentiment is a generic Advaita/perennialist formulation that appears in many unattributed forms. Absence from my knowledge is not proof the person does not exist, but there is no credible attribution to record here and no basis for a reattribution.

results.earliest_print_source: "Picasso Speaks," The Arts (New York), May 1923 — statement to Marius de Zayas
results.notes: Genuine Picasso, from his 1923 statement published as 'Picasso Speaks' in The Arts, given to Marius de Zayas. The original runs: 'We all know that Art is not truth. Art is a lie that makes us realize truth, at least the truth that is given us to understand.' The version here is the standard compressed paraphrase ('makes us realize the truth'), so the attribution is verified even though the wording is abridged. Author field should read 'Pablo Picasso' rather than the bare surname.

results.earliest_print_source: Republic, Plato, Book VII, ~536d–537a (paraphrase)
results.notes: This is a genuine Platonic position, loosely rendered. In Republic Book VII Socrates argues that early education should not be enforced by compulsion but conducted as play, because nothing learned under compulsion stays in the mind. The English here is a paraphrase rather than any standard translation (compare Jowett's 'do not use compulsion, but let early education be a sort of amusement'), so I am recording it as attributed to Plato in substance, not verified as a quotation.

A well-documented pseudo-Plato. This sentence does not appear anywhere in the Platonic corpus and has no Greek original; it is routinely listed among misattributed Plato quotations. Plato does discuss music's effect on the soul (Republic III, Timaeus), which is presumably how the line got attached to him, but the wording is modern and its actual author is unknown to me, so I am not offering a reattribution. Note this is a near-duplicate of q_1149, and this copy additionally contains a typo ('everthing').

results.earliest_print_source: Ian Maclaren (Rev. John Watson), c. 1897–1898 — 'Be pitiful, for every man is fighting a hard battle.'
results.notes: Not Plato. This is one of the best-known false Plato attributions; it appears in the misattributed section of Plato's Wikiquote page and has been traced by Quote Investigator to Ian Maclaren, the pen name of the Scottish author and clergyman John Watson, in the late 1890s, in the form 'Be pitiful, for every man is fighting a hard battle.' The modernized 'Be kind... everyone you meet' wording is a later drift. The quote has also been falsely credited to Philo of Alexandria and to J.M. Barrie. Recording the reattribution to Maclaren with high confidence.
results.suggested_reattribution: Ian Maclaren (pen name of Rev. John Watson)

results.notes: I cannot locate this sentence in any Platonic dialogue I know, and its phrasing is much closer to Stoicism — the claim that the free person remains free in chains is characteristically Epictetus (Discourses, Enchiridion), not Plato. Plato does argue that the tyrant is the true slave (Republic IX), but that is a different claim. I am not confident enough in a Stoic origin to assert a reattribution; I am confident enough to say the Plato attribution is unsupported.

results.earliest_print_source: Gorgias, Plato, ~380 BCE (474b–475e)
results.notes: Genuine and central Plato. In the Gorgias, Socrates argues against Polus that doing injustice is worse and more shameful than suffering it (the thesis is set out around 474b and argued through 475e, and echoed at 469b–c). The English here matches the standard translation family closely. Verified on the strength of the primary text.

results.earliest_print_source: Apology, Plato, ~399–390 BCE (38a)
results.notes: Plato's Apology 38a, spoken by Socrates at his trial — the standard English rendering of ho de anexetastos bios ou biotos anthropoi. Strictly the words are Socrates' as reported by Plato, so either attribution is defensible; crediting Plato (as author of the Apology) is conventional and correct, and I am not treating that as a misattribution.

Same pseudo-Plato as q_1144, in its cleaner and more commonly circulated form. No such passage exists in Plato's works and there is no Greek original; it is a standard entry in lists of misattributed Plato quotations. Origin of the English sentence is unknown to me, so no reattribution is offered. Flagging as a duplicate of q_1144 for deduplication.

Pythagoras left no writings, so every quotation credited to him is by definition secondhand, arriving through much later compilers (the Golden Verses, Stobaeus, Diogenes Laertius, Iamblichus) or through early-modern anthologies. This particular English sentence has the cadence of an eighteenth- or nineteenth-century maxim collection rather than a translation from a classical source, and I cannot place it in any ancient text. Attribution exists by convention only.

Consistently attributed to R. Buckminster Fuller across quotation collections and Fuller-related writing, and the phrasing matches his idiom (serendipity as method, 'precession'). I cannot place it in a specific book from memory — some collections point to his poetic works of the late 1960s/early 1970s, but I will not assert a title I cannot confirm. Attribution is stable and plausible; the primary source is unlocated.

The formulation is characteristic of R. H. Blyth, whose 'Zen in English Literature and Oriental Classics' (1942) and multi-volume 'Zen and Zen Classics' argue exactly this — that Zen strips the world of symbolic overlay. I recall the line circulating as Blyth's and believe the attribution is genuine, but I cannot pin the volume or page from memory and will not guess between the two works.

This is a known misattribution. The joy/service triplet is a 20th-century reworking of Ellen Sturgis Hooper's short poem published in The Dial (1840): 'I slept, and dreamed that life was Beauty; / I woke, and found that life was Duty.' The 'service was joy' variant has been floated under Tagore, Gandhi, and Kahlil Gibran in different collections — a spread that is itself diagnostic — and I know of no passage in Tagore's works containing it. Quote Investigator has treated this family of variants and traced it back to Hooper.
results.suggested_reattribution: Derived from Ellen Sturgis Hooper's 1840 poem ('I slept, and dreamed that life was Beauty'); the joy/service wording has no known author

results.notes: Almost certainly not Tagore. The diction is modern colloquial American English ('my own version of an optimist', 'something terrific'), incompatible with Tagore's register in either Bengali or his own English renderings. I recognize this as a Joan Rivers line, widely quoted from her later interviews and her writing on resilience; the Tagore label appears to be a quote-site scrambling. I am confident it is not Tagore and reasonably confident it is Rivers, though I cannot name the specific book or interview.

Consistent with Tagore's metaphysics as expressed in 'Sadhana: The Realisation of Life' (1913) and 'The Religion of Man' (1931), and the attribution to him is stable across collections. I cannot locate the sentence in a specific text from memory, so I will not name a source. Plausible and uncontested but unverified.

A genuine and much-cited Tagore line on education, used institutionally in connection with Santiniketan and Visva-Bharati. It comes from his essays on education (collections such as 'Personality' (1917) and the 'A Poet's School' material are the usual pointers), but I cannot fix the exact essay from memory and will not guess. Strong, consistent attribution; specific citation unlocated.

results.earliest_print_source: The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge, Rainer Maria Rilke, 1910
results.notes: From Rilke's novel 'Die Aufzeichnungen des Malte Laurids Brigge' (1910); Malte's observation that life offers no beginners' classes and demands the hardest thing immediately. Wording here matches the common English translations (Mitchell/Norton lineage). Confident in the work, so verified, though I cannot give a page.

results.earliest_print_source: Letters to a Young Poet (Briefe an einen jungen Dichter), Rainer Maria Rilke, letter of 23 April 1903; published 1929, M. D. Herter Norton translation 1934
results.notes: From Letters to a Young Poet — the letter containing the 'ripening like a tree' passage, in which Rilke advises Kappus to grow quietly and seriously and warns against looking outward for answers. The English here is the Norton translation, whose slightly archaic syntax ('I do only want to advise you') matches. Confident in the work and the correspondence; letter number given from memory as the third.

results.earliest_print_source: Letters to a Young Poet (Briefe an einen jungen Dichter), Rainer Maria Rilke, first letter, Paris, 17 February 1903; published 1929
