results.notes: From the opening letter to Franz Xaver Kappus, immediately following the 'go into yourself' advice: if everyday life seems poor, the fault lies with the poet's insufficiency, not the life. One of the most securely sourced passages in the Rilke corpus.

Reads as authentic Rilke prose from his correspondence — the paradox of love increasing by being given, tied to flowers and children, is his register and imagery. It circulates widely through John J. L. Mood's anthology 'Rilke on Love and Other Difficulties' (1975), which gathers passages from the letters. I cannot identify which letter it comes from, so I will not cite one. Genuine-seeming but unsourced.

results.earliest_print_source: Letters to a Young Poet (Briefe an einen jungen Dichter), Rainer Maria Rilke, letter of 16 July 1903, Worpswede; published 1929
results.notes: The 'live the questions now' passage — the single best-known paragraph in Letters to a Young Poet, from the fourth letter. The wording here is a modern English rendering (locked rooms / books in a foreign language / live your way into the answer) and the ellipses are the compiler's, but the passage is unambiguously Rilke's.

results.earliest_print_source: Das Stunden-Buch (The Book of Hours), Rainer Maria Rilke, 1905; English in Rilke's Book of Hours: Love Poems to God, trans. Anita Barrows and Joanna Macy, 1996
results.notes: Closing lines of the poem beginning 'Gott spricht zu jedem nur, eh er ihn macht' ('God speaks to each of us as he makes us') from the Book of Hours. German: 'Lass dir Alles geschehn: Schönheit und Schrecken. / Man muss nur gehn: Kein Gefühl ist das fernste.' The familiar English wording, including 'No feeling is final', is the Barrows/Macy translation — worth noting since the line is often quoted as if bare Rilke.

A popular verse-shaped collage rather than a translation. One sentence has a real source: 'The future enters into us, in order to transform itself in us, long before it happens' is from Letters to a Young Poet (the letter of 12 August 1904 in the standard sequence). The surrounding lines — 'You must give birth to your images', 'the hour of new clarity' — do not correspond to any standard translation I can recall, and the arrangement into short lines is a modern editorial creation. Rilkean in origin but not a quotable Rilke text as it stands.

Plausibly from Rilke's wartime or post-war correspondence, where he links inner freedom to peace, and the sentence structure suggests translated German. I cannot place it in any letter or published work, and it does not appear in the well-trodden Letters to a Young Poet material. Attribution is uncontested but I have no evidence for it.

Attributed consistently to Ralph W. Gerard, the American neurophysiologist, and the thought matches his published interest in the biology of imagination and creative thinking (he wrote on 'the biological basis of imagination' in the mid-1940s). The attribution is stable and the author obscure enough that misattribution pressure is low — nobody invents a quote to hang on Ralph Gerard. Specific source unlocated.

Ralph Marston writes The Daily Motivator, a long-running series of short daily messages, and this is characteristic of that output in both voice and structure. Attribution to Marston is consistent wherever it appears. Individual Daily Motivator entries are dated but I cannot supply the date from memory, so no citation is given.

The 'What is Success?' passage — one of the most thoroughly documented Emerson misattributions. It originates with Bessie Anderson Stanley, whose prize-winning 1904 contest entry read 'He has achieved success who has lived well, laughed often, and loved much...'. The version here is a mid-20th-century expansion (the 'healthy child, a garden patch, a redeemed social condition' clauses are later accretions) that acquired Emerson's name in anthologies and greeting cards. It appears in no edition of Emerson's works. Emerson scholars and Quote Investigator both reject the attribution.
results.suggested_reattribution: Bessie Anderson Stanley (1904), in an evolved and expanded form by later hands

results.notes: Not found in Emerson's published works, journals, or letters as far as I know; the Emerson attribution is a 20th-century label with no textual support. The thought and structure track e. e. cummings closely: 'To be nobody-but-yourself in a world which is doing its best, night and day, to make you everybody else means to fight the hardest battle which any human being can fight' (A Poet's Advice to Students, 1955). The circulating 'Emerson' sentence looks like a compressed rewording of cummings. Emerson is a misattribution magnet for self-reliance aphorisms precisely because 'Self-Reliance' makes the sentiment sound like his.
results.suggested_reattribution: Probably a compressed rewording of e. e. cummings, 'A Poet's Advice to Students' (1955)

results.notes: I believe this is genuine Emerson, but the canonical wording carries an extra word: 'A good intention clothes itself with sudden power.' The dropped 'sudden' suggests transmission through a quote collection rather than the text. My recollection places it in the Essays: First Series (1841) period, most likely 'Spiritual Laws', but I am not certain enough of the essay to cite it, and naming the wrong essay would be worse than naming none.

Genuine Emerson prose in my judgment — the passage continues '...all opportunities, strings of tension waiting to be struck', a cadence and image that belong to him and that no anthologist would invent. My recollection associates it with the later essays, 'Works and Days' in Society and Solitude (1870) being the most likely home, but I cannot confirm the essay and so leave the citation blank. Note the quote as given truncates the passage mid-thought.

results.earliest_print_source: Nature, Ralph Waldo Emerson, 1836
results.notes: From Emerson's first book, 'Nature' (1836), in the closing chapter 'Prospects'. The sentence is quoted accurately here and sits in the passage arguing that wisdom consists in perceiving the miraculous within the ordinary — the culminating movement of the essay.

Universally attributed to Emerson and entirely consistent with his thought, but I cannot place it in any essay, and its compact epigram form is the shape misattributions usually take. It may come from his journals, which are less well indexed in quote culture and therefore both a plausible home and a convenient one. Holding below the promotion bar until a text can be pointed to.

Circulates almost exclusively as Emerson, and occasionally as an anonymous proverb. I cannot locate it in his essays or journals, and the neat paradox reads more like a 19th- or 20th-century aphorism collection than like Emerson's sentence rhythm, which rarely lands this tidily. No evidence against him either — the honest verdict is that I do not know.

Doubtful as Emerson. I know of no passage in his published works containing it. In 20th-century usage the line is most strongly associated with the historian Charles A. Beard, who offered it as one of his 'lessons of history', and it was later used by Martin Luther King Jr.; both are transmitters rather than demonstrable origins. Related dark/stars proverbs predate all of them, so the true source may be proverbial. Treating this as unverified rather than reattributed because I cannot identify who said it first.

results.earliest_print_source: The Conduct of Life, Ralph Waldo Emerson, 1860
results.notes: Genuine Emerson, from The Conduct of Life (1860); my recollection places it in the essay 'Worship'. One wording note: the canonical text reads 'where every one hides his real character, and reveals it by hiding' — the quote here has 'his own character', a small corruption worth correcting against the printed text before promotion.

This is the well-documented 'Success' poem misattribution. Emerson never wrote it; it appears in the Misattributed section of his Wikiquote page and has been traced by Quote Investigator to a 1904 prize-winning contest entry by Bessie Anderson Stanley ('He has achieved success who has lived well, laughed often, and loved much...'). The 'To laugh often and much / to win the respect of intelligent people' wording is a much later 20th-century rewrite of Stanley's text, circulated anonymously before being pinned on Emerson. I am confident it is not Emerson; I am less confident about who produced this specific rewrite.
results.suggested_reattribution: Bessie Anderson Stanley (1904), heavily reworded by an unknown later hand

results.notes: Consistently attributed to Emerson across anthologies and stylistically authentic to him (the cadence and the 'this hour's duties' construction are characteristic). I cannot place the specific essay, address, or journal entry from memory, so I am not asserting a print source. Attribution is plausible and stable but unverified at the primary-source level.

Extremely common in quote collections under Emerson's name, but I cannot recall it in any of his essays, addresses, or journals. Emerson is a moderate misattribution magnet for aphoristic one-liners of this shape. The epigram feels more like late-19th/early-20th-century American maxim writing than Emerson's own prose. No source found in training knowledge; treat the attribution as unsupported rather than disproven.

results.earliest_print_source: Letters and Social Aims, Ralph Waldo Emerson, 1876 (essay 'Progress of Culture')
results.notes: I recall this line being cited to Emerson's 'Progress of Culture,' the Phi Beta Kappa address delivered at Harvard in July 1867 and collected in Letters and Social Aims (1876). The sentiment ('thoughts rule the world') is squarely Emerson's and I have reasonable confidence in the placement, but I am reporting a recollection, not a checked citation — the essay attribution should be confirmed against the text before the source line is trusted.

results.earliest_print_source: Essays: First Series ('Compensation'), Ralph Waldo Emerson, 1841
results.notes: Genuine Emerson, from the essay 'Compensation' in Essays: First Series (1841). The wording here matches the essay text closely ('It is one of the most beautiful compensations of this life, that no man can sincerely try to help another without helping himself'). This is one of the few heavily circulated Emerson lines with a solid primary source.

I am confident this is genuine Emerson prose — the fuller passage runs '...what deafness, what stone-blind custom, what overgrown error you behold is there only by sufferance — your sufferance. See it to be a lie, and you have already dealt it its mortal blow.' My recollection points to 'Compensation' (Essays: First Series, 1841), but I am not confident enough in the essay placement to record it as a citation. The ellipsis in the corpus text also elides an intervening clause.

Ralph Waldo Trine is a real New Thought author (1866-1958) and the vocabulary here — 'the all-pervading wisdom and power,' oneness, higher laws — is his signature phrasing, strongly suggesting In Tune with the Infinite (1897). I cannot place the passage precisely enough to assert the book and page, so no print source is recorded. Note the author is distinct from Ralph Waldo Emerson; the corpus has them adjacent and they are frequently confused.

Ubiquitously attributed to Ram Dass (born Richard Alpert) and consistent with his teaching, but I know of no primary source — no book passage, lecture transcript, or dated talk. It circulated widely as poster and software-splash-screen text before most quote sites indexed it, which is a typical pattern for floating attributions. Also note the corpus spells the author 'Ram Das'; the standard spelling is 'Ram Dass'.

This does not read as Ram Dass; it reads as Advaita source material. I recall this wording — 'All spiritual practices are done with a view to still the mind. The perfectly still mind is universal spirit' — from Nisargadatta Maharaj's I Am That, the Maurice Frydman translation. My confidence in the reattribution is moderate (roughly 0.6), not high, and it could alternatively trace to Ramana Maharshi's recorded talks, which share this idiom. Either way the Ram Dass attribution looks incorrect.

A genuinely Ram Dass-sounding line, usually quoted as 'The next message you need is always right where you are.' It is associated with his talks and with the Be Here Now era, and the attribution is stable across sources, but I cannot point to a book, transcript, or date. Attribution plausible, evidence thin. Author name should be 'Ram Dass'.

This 'I honor the place in you...' gloss on Namaste is most often credited to Ram Dass and does match his idiom and his role in popularizing the greeting for Western audiences. However the same passage circulates attributed to Mahatma Gandhi and to anonymous yoga-studio tradition, which is a warning sign. No primary text or talk identified in my training knowledge. Author name should be 'Ram Dass'.

'Rama Choomarasawmy' is not a real person — it is a phonetic corruption of Ananda K. Coomaraswamy (1877-1947), the Ceylonese-British metaphysician and art historian. The passage is characteristic Coomaraswamy, from his writing on traditional art and the artist's identification with the form contemplated; my recollection points toward The Transformation of Nature in Art (1934) or Christian and Oriental Philosophy of Art (1943), but I cannot fix the book, so no print source is recorded. Confidence in the author correction is high (~0.85); confidence in the recorded name as given is near zero. Note also 'The artists is' in the corpus text is a typo for 'The artist is'.

The musk-deer parable — the deer roaming in search of a fragrance emanating from its own navel — is a genuine and very old motif in Indian devotional literature, used by Kabir, by Ramakrishna, and in later Vedanta teaching. Ramakrishna did employ it, so the attribution is not baseless, but this compressed English sentence is an anthologist's paraphrase rather than a line from The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna as far as I can tell. The image is effectively traditional and predates any single speaker.

Consistent with Ramana Maharshi's recorded teaching on silence as the highest and most potent form of instruction, and I associate this passage with Talks with Sri Ramana Maharshi (Munagala Venkataramiah's transcripts) or Maharshi's Gospel. The usual ordering in his teaching runs silence to ego to thought to speech, matching this text. I cannot cite a specific talk number, so no print source is recorded.

results.earliest_print_source: 'G.B.S. — Mark V' (short story), Ray Bradbury, 1976, collected in Long After Midnight
results.notes: Genuinely Bradbury, and unmistakably his voice. I recall the passage as spoken by the George Bernard Shaw robot in the short story 'G.B.S. — Mark V,' collected in Long After Midnight (1976); Bradbury also reused the 'the Universe has shouted itself alive, we are one of the shouts' formulation in essays and interviews. Confidence in Bradbury as author is high; confidence in the specific story placement is somewhat lower and worth confirming against the text.

'Raymond Inmon' appears in my knowledge only as a name attached to this one sentence in motivational quote collections — no biography, no book, no other work, no dates. That pattern usually indicates either a private individual quoted once in a newsletter or a name that accreted to an orphan line. The quote itself is real and widely circulated; the attribution is untraceable. Honest answer here is that I do not know who said it.

Reggie Leach is a real person — NHL winger, 'the Riverton Rifle,' Philadelphia Flyers — and this line is attributed to him with near-total consistency across motivational anthologies, which is mild evidence. But I know of no interview, book, or speech where it originates, and no date. Sports one-liners of this kind are commonly attached to whichever athlete an anthologist had to hand. Plausible but unverified.

Mary Manin Morrissey is a real New Thought/Unity minister and author (Building Your Field of Dreams, 1996) and the language here — 'Spirit has placed a dream in your heart' — matches her register exactly, so the attribution is plausible. But it reads like newsletter or spoken-message material rather than a passage from a specific book, and I cannot locate it. No source recorded.

Cecil Williams of Glide Memorial in San Francisco may well have said this from the pulpit, but he did not originate it. The aphorism is centuries older and circulates in two mirrored forms: 'Pray as though everything depended on God, work as though everything depended on you,' commonly credited to Ignatius of Loyola and also to Augustine of Hippo. Scholarship on the Ignatian version (Joseph de Guibert and others) notes the two halves get swapped between retellings, which is itself evidence of a long oral history. Treat this as a traditional Christian saying quoted by Williams, not authored by him.
results.suggested_reattribution: Traditional Christian aphorism, commonly attributed to Ignatius of Loyola

results.notes: Widely quoted under Richard Avedon's name in design and photography collections, and the sentiment fits a working photographer's outlook. I cannot place it in an Avedon interview, essay, or monograph, and I have some recollection of near-identical 'style is chains, ideas are freedom' formulations circulating under other designers' names, which weakens confidence. Attribution plausible but unsupported.

results.earliest_print_source: Illusions: The Adventures of a Reluctant Messiah, Richard Bach, 1977
results.notes: Genuine Bach, from Illusions: The Adventures of a Reluctant Messiah (1977), where it appears as one of the aphorisms in the Messiah's Handbook. Attribution is solid and the source is well established in the secondary literature. Occasionally seen paraphrased as 'What the caterpillar calls the end of the world, the master calls a butterfly' — same source.

Consistently attributed to Richard Bach and consonant with the Messiah's Handbook aphorisms in Illusions (1977), which is my best guess for the source. I am noticeably less confident than for the caterpillar line — I cannot confirm the book, and the sentiment is generic enough that it could belong to the broader 'those who think they can' tradition running back to Virgil's 'possunt quia posse videntur.' No print source recorded.

Richard Carlson is a real author (Don't Sweat the Small Stuff, 1997, and its many sequels) and this sentence is consistent with his advice register, but it is generic enough that it could come from almost any business or self-help writer. I cannot place it in a specific title or chapter. Plausible attribution, no evidence.

Attributed with good consistency to Richard M. DeVos, Amway co-founder, and the 'Here comes number seventy-one' formulation is distinctive enough that it is unlikely to have drifted from another speaker. It matches the content of his motivational speaking and his book Believe! (1975), which is my best guess for the source, but I cannot confirm the book or a speech date, so no print source is recorded. Note the corpus name should probably be punctuated 'Richard M. DeVos'.

Attributed to Richard Nelson Bolles, author of What Color Is Your Parachute?, and it strongly matches his voice and his argument against 'realistic' career advice; my recollection is that it appears in the book, whose editions run annually from 1970, but I cannot pin an edition or page and will not guess a year. The closing image, 'gave them horses to ride,' echoes the old proverb 'if wishes were horses, beggars would ride,' which Bolles was plausibly inverting deliberately. Attribution stable, primary source unconfirmed.

Richard Schechner is a real and well-documented performance studies theorist (Environmental Theater, Performance Theory, Between Theater and Anthropology), but I cannot place this specific sentence in any of his writings. The register is more aphoristic than Schechner's usual analytic prose, which makes me mildly suspicious that it entered quote collections secondhand. No source located; not fabricating one.

Consistent in voice and content with Robert A. Johnson's Jungian writing on love, most plausibly 'We: Understanding the Psychology of Romantic Love' (1983), which argues precisely this distinction between love as a doing and love as a state of being. I have a genuine but not firm recollection of the passage from that book, and cannot confirm chapter or page, so I am leaving the print source null rather than asserting a citation I cannot stand behind. Attribution to Johnson itself is plausible and consistently reported.

Consistently attributed to Robert G. Allen, the real-estate and 'Multiple Streams of Income' author, across business quote collections. The sentiment matches his investing rhetoric. However, every occurrence I know of is a quote-collection citation with no book or page, so this is secondary evidence only. Note the ambiguity of the bare name 'Robert Allen' — the corpus should probably disambiguate to Robert G. Allen.

I cannot place this line in Robert G. Allen's published work. It circulates in motivational-quote lists with the bare name 'Robert Allen' attached. Generic enough in phrasing that it could belong to any number of sales/persistence writers. No traceable source; honest answer is that I do not know.

This is a composite passage, not a single quote, and that matters. The inner quotation is credited in the text itself to Herb True (the Notre Dame marketing professor), and the 'more failures than failures do' line is indeed the one commonly attributed to him. The closing 'You don't drown by falling in the water. You drown by staying there' is widely attributed elsewhere to Edwin Louis Cole. The framing prose is plausibly Robert G. Allen quoting both, likely in one of his books, but I cannot confirm which. Recommend the corpus either drop this entry or split it, since attributing the whole block to Allen misrepresents two embedded attributions.

Widely attributed to Robert Browning in nineteenth- and twentieth-century quote anthologies, but I cannot locate it in any specific poem or letter of his, and Browning's actual verse rarely reduces to a clean epigram like this. The same line also circulates attributed to Samuel Johnson in some collections, which is a classic signature of an unsourced anthology quote drifting between famous names. Attribution unresolved.

I recall this line, usually punctuated as three sentences ('Progress is a nice word. But change is its motivator. And change has its enemies.'), from Robert F. Kennedy's Day of Affirmation Address at the University of Cape Town, 6 June 1966 — the same speech as the 'ripple of hope' passage. The attribution to RFK is consistent and I consider it sound. I am withholding the speech as a formal print source because I cannot confirm the exact verbatim placement from memory, which is the difference between 'attributed' and 'verified' here.

results.earliest_print_source: A Witness Tree, Robert Frost, 1942
results.notes: This is not merely a line by Frost — it is the title of his poem 'Happiness Makes Up in Height for What It Lacks in Length,' collected in A Witness Tree (1942), the volume that won him his fourth Pulitzer. Attribution is secure and the source is a published primary text.

results.earliest_print_source: North of Boston, Robert Frost, 1914 (poem: 'A Servant to Servants')
results.notes: From the dramatic monologue 'A Servant to Servants' in North of Boston (1914), where the speaker reports her husband's saying: 'He says the best way out is always through.' Worth noting for corpus honesty that in context the line is a character quoting another character, not Frost speaking in his own voice — but the wording and the source are secure.

The plainspoken, self-deprecating voice is very much Robert Fulghum's, and the content fits his essay collections (All I Really Need to Know I Learned in Kindergarten, From Beginning to End, Words I Wish I Wrote). But I cannot place the passage in a specific book, and it reads like it may come from an interview rather than a book. Plausible but unsourced.

Squarely in the idiom of Robert H. Schuller's 'possibility thinking' and consistently attributed to him in inspirational collections; the sentence is essentially a compressed statement of his central theme (cf. 'Tough Times Never Last, But Tough People Do!'). No specific book, sermon, or Hour of Power broadcast identified, so this rests on secondary evidence only.

results.earliest_print_source: The Art Spirit, Robert Henri (compiled by Margery Ryerson), 1923
results.notes: A well-established line from The Art Spirit (1923), the collection of Henri's teaching notes and letters assembled by his student Margery Ryerson. Usually quoted as 'The object isn't to make art, it's to be in that wonderful state which makes art inevitable.' The submitted text substitutes 'the' for 'that,' a trivial variant. Attribution and source are solid; I hold at 0.85 rather than higher only because I cannot cite the page.

Robert L. Peters is a real Canadian graphic designer and past president of Icograda, and this three-clause line is his best-known statement — it is quoted consistently under his name throughout design literature and conference material, and he has spoken about it publicly as his own. I have no single originating publication or talk to cite, so it stays at 'attributed' rather than 'verified,' but the attribution itself is unusually stable for a design aphorism.

Very widely attributed to Robert Louis Stevenson (usually as 'Saints are sinners who kept on going'), but I cannot locate it in any of his essays, novels, letters, or prayers. Its circulation pattern — heavy in devotional and recovery literature, absent from Stevenson scholarship — is characteristic of an unsourced attribution attached to a famous literary name. I do not know a true origin, so I am not proposing a reattribution, but the Stevenson claim should be treated as doubtful.

results.earliest_print_source: Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance: An Inquiry into Values, Robert M. Pirsig, 1974
results.notes: A genuine and well-known line from Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance (1974), from the mountain-climbing passages in which the narrator reflects on Chris and on the futility of treating the summit as the point. Attribution and source both secure.

The 'grain of sand in your shoe' image is attributed to the Yukon poet Robert W. Service in many quote collections, but I cannot find it in his verse or his memoirs, and the surrounding sentence ('Be master of your petty annoyances...') reads like self-help prose rather than Service. A near-identical formulation is widely credited to Muhammad Ali ('It isn't the mountains ahead to climb that wear you out; it's the pebble in your shoe'), which suggests a floating aphorism rather than a fixed authorship. Origin genuinely unclear; not proposing Ali either, since his version is also unsourced.

I have no knowledge of Roberta Sage Hamilton as a writer and can find no work of hers in my training. The passage appears to live entirely inside inspirational quote collections and greeting-card style compilations. The name may be real but obscure, or may itself be a corruption. No verification possible; this is an honest 'I do not know.'

results.earliest_print_source: Histoire amoureuse des Gaules, Roger de Rabutin, Comte de Bussy, 1665
results.notes: A genuine and long-established maxim of Bussy-Rabutin — 'L'absence est à l'amour ce qu'est au feu le vent: il éteint le petit, il allume le grand' — standardly cited to Histoire amoureuse des Gaules (1665). One housekeeping note for the corpus: the author name should be 'Roger de Bussy-Rabutin' or, more properly, 'Roger de Rabutin, Comte de Bussy'; the submitted 'Roger DeBussy-Rabutin' garbles the particle and should be corrected.
results.suggested_reattribution: Roger de Rabutin, Comte de Bussy (Bussy-Rabutin)

results.notes: 'Roger Williams' is ambiguous and none of the candidates resolve it. The seventeenth-century founder of Rhode Island would not have written in this idiom of self-actualization; the biochemist Roger J. Williams and the pianist Roger Williams are both possible but I have no evidence for either. The vocabulary ('developing your potential') places the line in twentieth-century human-potential writing. Untraceable as given.

Ron Rathbun is a real author — 'The Way Is Within: A Spiritual Journey' (1995) and related meditation writing — and this line is attributed to him with reasonable consistency in quote collections. I cannot confirm it against the book itself, and the sentiment is generic enough to have multiple independent origins. Plausible but unverified.

Same author and same situation as the preceding entry: consistently attributed to Ron Rathbun in quote compilations, consistent with the plain instructional voice of 'The Way Is Within,' but with no source I can confirm. Weak evidence.

Rosemary Fillmore Rhea is a real figure — granddaughter of Unity's founders Charles and Myrtle Fillmore, and a Unity broadcaster and author — and the New Thought vocabulary of 'collective consciousness' fits Unity writing closely. But I cannot place this sentence in any of her books or broadcasts. Attribution plausible on stylistic grounds only.

Attributed to Rousseau in quote collections, but I cannot locate it in the Discourses, Émile, the Social Contract, or the Reveries. Two warning signs: the English is awkward in the way that anthology-chain translations tend to be (the missing comma before 'is in us' is present in most circulating copies, indicating they all descend from one source), and the bare author name 'Rousseau' with no first name is typical of unsourced compilation entries. The sentiment is broadly Rousseauian, which is exactly what makes a misattribution easy. I do not know the true origin.

results.earliest_print_source: A House with Four Rooms, Rumer Godden, 1989
results.notes: This passage is securely associated with the novelist Rumer Godden, who grew up in India; she used the four-rooms image as the epigraph and title source of 'A House with Four Rooms' (1989), the second volume of her autobiography. Note that Godden is relaying a belief she attributes to an Indian source rather than claiming the thought as her own, so the corpus should present her as the one who recorded it. Attribution to Godden is strong; I hold just at the promotion threshold because I cannot confirm the exact wording against the printed epigraph.

Rumi is one of the strongest misattribution magnets in circulation, and the English Rumi corpus is dominated by Coleman Barks's loose renderings, which are not translations and often have no close counterpart in the Persian. I cannot match this line to any passage of the Masnavi or the Divan-e Shams that I know. The bread-and-hunger image is genuinely Rumi-adjacent in theme, which is not evidence. Treat as unverified pending a check against a scholarly translation (Nicholson or Arberry) with a book-and-line reference.

results.earliest_print_source: The Essential Rumi, trans. Coleman Barks, 1995
results.notes: From the Barks rendering beginning 'Today, like every other day, we wake up empty and frightened... Take down a musical instrument. Let the beauty we love be what we do. There are hundreds of ways to kneel and kiss the ground.' The corpus text alters 'we love' to 'you love', a common web variant. Barks worked from earlier English translations rather than the Persian, so the English wording is his; the underlying poem is genuinely Rumi's. Cannot place the Persian original (Divan-e Shams ghazal) from memory.

results.earliest_print_source: The Essential Rumi, trans. Coleman Barks, 1995
results.notes: A Barks rendering of a Rumi quatrain; I recall it in The Essential Rumi with consistent attribution across reputable Rumi collections. Wording is Barks' English, not a literal translation. No Persian source located from memory.

I cannot place this line in any Rumi translation I know — not Barks, Nicholson, Arberry, or Helminski. The theological compression ('you must become God') is unlike the standard renderings, which speak of annihilation in the Beloved rather than becoming God. Possibly a loose paraphrase of a fana passage, possibly a modern invention. Honest answer: unknown.

Cannot place this in any Rumi translation. The grain-of-sand-becomes-pearl motif is a stock modern inspirational image; the flat declarative diction here matches none of the standard English Rumi translators. Circulates on quote sites without any cited source. Likely a modern composition attached to Rumi's name, but I have no evidence of a true author.

Rumi does use the rider-who-cannot-see-his-own-mount figure (the Mathnawi has teaching stories about a man searching for the animal he is riding), so the image is authentically Rumi's. But I cannot place this exact English sentence in any translation, and it reads like a paraphrase rather than a rendering. Image plausible, wording unverified.

results.earliest_print_source: The Essential Rumi, trans. Coleman Barks, 1995
results.notes: A well-known Barks rendering of a Rumi quatrain, appearing in The Essential Rumi. Attribution to Rumi is consistent across reputable collections; the English phrasing ('Lovers don't finally meet somewhere. They're in each other all along.') is Barks'. Persian original not identified from memory.

I recall this short line from Coleman Barks' Rumi versions and believe it appears in The Essential Rumi, but I am not confident enough in the specific volume to cite it as a print source. Attribution to Rumi (via Barks) is consistent in the sources I know; the underlying Persian is not identified.

One of the most heavily circulated 'Rumi' lines on the internet and one of the most doubted. I cannot place it in Barks, Nicholson, Arberry, Helminski, or any other translation, and its vocabulary ('your task', 'barriers within yourself') is modern therapeutic English rather than Sufi poetics — it reads closer to twentieth-century self-help or A Course in Miracles-adjacent writing than to a thirteenth-century ghazal. I suspect it is not Rumi, but I cannot name a true author, so I am not asserting a reattribution.

I have a weak recollection of this line in a Barks-style Rumi rendering (sometimes quoted with a following sentence about the body's purity), but I cannot confirm the volume or the Persian original. The imagery is consistent with Rumi's treatment of the body as woven of light. Attribution plausible, evidence thin.

Among the most quoted Rumi lines in English, and consistently attributed to him via Coleman Barks' versions. However, Rumi scholars (Omid Safi among them) have noted that Barks' most famous lines often have no close Persian counterpart, and I cannot point to the ghazal or Mathnawi passage behind this one. Attribution is consistent but the sourcing chain stops at a modern English rendering, so I am not putting it above the promotion bar.

Cannot place this line. Alchemical gold imagery is genuinely Rumi's territory (the Beloved as the philosopher's stone that transmutes copper to gold), but this specific one-sentence formulation appears only on quote aggregators with no source. Unknown.

results.earliest_print_source: The Essential Rumi, trans. Coleman Barks, 1995
results.notes: A recognized Coleman Barks rendering ('Dance, when you're broken open...'), appearing in The Essential Rumi and widely reprinted with consistent attribution to Rumi. English wording is Barks'; Persian original not identified from memory.

results.earliest_print_source: "No Frames, No Boundaries," Russell Schweickart, address to the Lindisfarne Association, July 1974
results.notes: This is the well-documented passage from Apollo 9 astronaut Rusty Schweickart's 1974 Lindisfarne talk 'No Frames, No Boundaries,' delivered in the second person as he recounts his EVA and the view of Earth. It has been reprinted many times, including in Lindisfarne conference collections and in Kevin Kelley's photo-and-text anthology The Home Planet (1988). I am confident of the speaker and the talk; I am less certain of which reprint carries this exact excerpt, so I have cited the original address rather than a page. Note the corpus author field carries the redundant title suffix 'Astronaut'.

Sabrina Ward Harrison is a real author-artist (Spilling Open: The Art of Becoming Yourself, 1999; Brave on the Rocks, 2000), and this aphorism's register fits her handwritten-journal books. But I cannot place the line in a specific title, and the thought is a commonplace of Buddhist-inflected popular writing, so it could easily have drifted onto her name. Unconfirmed.

This does not read as Augustine in any register — not the Confessions, not the City of God, not the sermons — and 'a life worth remembering' as a route to 'immortality' inverts Augustine's actual theology, where immortality is God's gift and earthly fame is explicitly disparaged. The line circulates far more commonly attributed to Bruce Lee, in the sayings collected from his notebooks and popularized posthumously; that attribution is itself unverified, so I am flagging the Augustine attribution as wrong without asserting Lee as confirmed.
results.suggested_reattribution: Widely circulated as Bruce Lee (that attribution is itself unverified); not Augustine

results.notes: Consistently attributed to Salvador Dali across quotation dictionaries and Dali literature, and the sentiment matches his public persona of grandiose self-deprecation. I cannot name the interview, book, or date of first appearance, so the sourcing chain is secondary only. Attribution steady, primary source not established.

Johnson wrote at length on fear in The Rambler (No. 126 contains the well-known 'Fear is implanted in us as a preservative from evil; but its duty, like that of other passions, is not to overbear reason, but to assist it'), and this sentence is stylistically compatible with that essay. But the crisp epigrammatic form suggests a later condensation of Johnson's prose rather than his own sentence, and I cannot confirm the exact wording in any Rambler or Idler number. Plausible but unconfirmed; deliberately not citing a number I cannot verify.

results.earliest_print_source: The Idler, No. 58, Samuel Johnson, 1759
results.notes: Genuine Johnson, from The Idler essay on the disappointment of anticipated pleasures. The original punctuates it as two sentences ('Pleasure is very seldom found where it is sought. Our brightest blazes of gladness are commonly kindled by unexpected sparks.'); the corpus joins them with a semicolon. I am confident of the essay and confident of Johnson; the 1759 date follows the Idler's run in the Universal Chronicle.

results.earliest_print_source: Recollections of the Table-Talk of Samuel Rogers, Alexander Dyce, 1856
results.notes: A stock Regency epigram consistently credited to the poet and celebrated conversationalist Samuel Rogers (1763-1855), whose remarks survive chiefly through Dyce's posthumous Table-Talk. Quotation dictionaries routinely source Rogers quips to that volume and I believe this is one of them, but I cannot confirm the page or that this specific quip appears there rather than in another memoir of Rogers, so treat the citation as probable rather than checked.

Attributed only to an anonymous collective ('Samurai maxim'), which is not an attribution at all. I cannot trace it to Hagakure, the Book of Five Rings, Budoshoshinshu, or any classical bushido text, and the English is modern. Most 'samurai maxims' in circulation are twentieth-century Western compositions. Origin unknown.

Sanaya Roman and Duane Packer are real co-authors whose Creating Money: Keys to Abundance (1988) covers exactly this material, so the pairing of quote to authors is plausible. I cannot confirm this sentence appears in that book or in another of their titles. Also note the author field misspells the second name as 'Duane Pack' (should be Duane Packer) and so does not match q_1248's spelling.

Consistent in content and voice with the Roman/Packer Earth Life Series (Creating Money, Living with Joy, Spiritual Growth), but I cannot place the sentence in a specific volume or year. Real authors, plausible attribution, no confirmable source.

Sandra Anne Taylor is a real author (Quantum Success, Secrets of Attraction, Truth, Triumph and Transformation) and the vocabulary of 'self-honoring choices' and 'authentic power' fits that genre and era. I cannot locate this passage in any specific title of hers. Unconfirmed. The corpus text also retains stray enclosing quotation marks and an anomalous capital after a semicolon.

Widely circulated with consistent attribution to Sara Paddison, and usually to her book The Hidden Power of the Heart (Planetary Publications / HeartMath, 1992), which is a real title on exactly this subject. I have not confirmed the page or verified the excerpt against the text, so I am recording the attribution as consistent secondary evidence rather than citing the book as a checked source. The trailing ellipsis indicates the passage is truncated.

Same author and same idiom as q_1250 — the heart-intelligence language ('surrender your head to your heart', 'the real teacher is within you') is characteristic HeartMath-school writing and consistent with Sara Paddison's The Hidden Power of the Heart (1992). But this longer passage is less commonly quoted than q_1250 and I cannot place it in a specific chapter or confirm it is not stitched together from separate paragraphs. Plausible, unconfirmed.

Consistently attributed to Sarah Ban Breathnach and entirely consistent with her vocabulary in the Simple Abundance books ('authentic', noticing ordinary days). I believe it comes from Simple Abundance: A Daybook of Comfort and Joy (1995) or a companion volume, but I cannot place the specific entry or page from memory, so I am not asserting that citation. Attribution to Breathnach is plausible and uncontested; the sourcing is not established.

Very widely and consistently attributed to Sarah Bernhardt in twentieth-century quotation anthologies, but in my recollection it circulates without a source citation — it is the kind of line that appears in quote dictionaries with only a name attached. Bernhardt did publish a memoir (Ma Double Vie / Memories of My Life, 1907), and the line would not be out of character, but I cannot confirm it appears there. Honest verdict: plausible, unsourced.

Circulates widely in Sathya Sai Baba devotional literature and is stylistically characteristic of his discourses. His discourses were transcribed at length in the Sathya Sai Speaks series, so a genuine origin is plausible, but I cannot identify the specific discourse, date, or volume, and Sai Baba material is heavily paraphrased and re-edited in secondary circulation. No citation asserted.

Ubiquitous on design quote lists under Saul Bass, but I know of no documented primary source — no interview, lecture, or published essay of his that I can point to containing this sentence. Design aphorisms attach themselves to famous designers (Bass, Rand, Eames) the way general aphorisms attach to Einstein, so the popularity of the pairing is not evidence. Cannot confirm or reattribute.

Saul Gorn was a real computer scientist at the University of Pennsylvania, known in hacker folklore for 'Saul Gorn's Compendium of Rarely Used Clichés.' This line reaches modern circulation almost entirely through the Unix fortune-cookie database, which is a weak provenance chain — fortune files carry many attributions that were never checked. I cannot place the line in anything Gorn actually published. Plausible but essentially unsourced.

Same fortune-file provenance problem as q_1256, and weaker: this is a generic optimism line with nothing distinctive tying it to Saul Gorn. I have no independent knowledge of Gorn saying or writing it, and I have a vague sense the sentence also circulates under other names, though I cannot confirm which and will not guess. Attribution should be treated as unsupported.

results.earliest_print_source: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter 6, Seneca the Younger, c. 65 CE
results.notes: Genuine Seneca. Letter 6 ('On Sharing Knowledge') contains 'nullius boni sine socio iucunda possessio est' — rendered by Gummere as 'no good thing is pleasant to possess, without friends to share it,' and by Robin Campbell (Penguin) along the lines of 'there is no enjoying the possession of anything valuable unless one has someone to share it with.' The English here is a compressed paraphrase rather than a standard translation, so the wording is loose even though the source is solid. Note also that the record's context field says 'Ancient Greek' — Seneca was Roman, writing in Latin; that field should be corrected.

results.earliest_print_source: Hsin Hsin Ming (Verses on the Faith Mind), traditionally ascribed to Jianzhi Sengcan, c. 6th-7th century; English wording from the Richard B. Clarke translation
results.notes: Both halves are from the Hsin Hsin Ming, and the phrasing matches the Richard B. Clarke translation, which is the version that dominates English circulation. The traditional ascription to Sengcan, the Third Chan/Zen Patriarch, is standard but scholarly consensus doubts he actually wrote it — the text is generally dated after his lifetime. So: the document is real and the quote is genuinely in it; the named author is traditional rather than established. The two sentences are also non-adjacent in the poem and have been stitched with an ellipsis.

results.earliest_print_source: Hsin Hsin Ming (Verses on the Faith Mind), traditionally ascribed to Jianzhi Sengcan, c. 6th-7th century; English wording from the Richard B. Clarke translation
results.notes: From the opening passage of the Hsin Hsin Ming, following 'The Great Way is not difficult for those who have no preferences' and 'If you wish to see the truth then hold no opinions for or against anything.' The line renders the Chinese 違順相爭 是為心病. Same caveat as q_1259: authorship by Sengcan is the traditional ascription, not a scholarly one.

results.earliest_print_source: Hsin Hsin Ming (Verses on the Faith Mind), traditionally ascribed to Jianzhi Sengcan, c. 6th-7th century; English wording from the Richard B. Clarke translation
results.notes: The closing lines of the Hsin Hsin Ming in Clarke's translation run 'Words! The Way is beyond language, for in it there is no yesterday, no tomorrow, no today.' The quote is that ending stripped of its frame, which makes it read as a standalone aphorism rather than the conclusion of an argument about the limits of language. Source is solid; the isolation changes the sense somewhat. Traditional-ascription caveat applies as in q_1259.

results.earliest_print_source: Hsin Hsin Ming (Verses on the Faith Mind), traditionally ascribed to Jianzhi Sengcan, c. 6th-7th century
results.notes: A well-known line of the Hsin Hsin Ming. Clarke renders it 'Do not search for the truth; only cease to cherish opinions'; the 'Don't seek reality, just put an end to opinions' wording comes from a different English translation of the same passage, which I cannot pin to a specific translator from memory. The underlying text and the ascription are the same as for q_1259 through q_1261.

Almost certainly a translation of the Hsin Hsin Ming line more commonly rendered 'Stop talking and thinking, and there is nothing you will not be able to know' (Suzuki/Conze) — the sense and position in the poem match. But I cannot identify which translation produces this exact English, and 'step aside from all thinking' is loose enough that it may be a popular paraphrase rather than a published rendering. Source text is confident; this specific wording is not, so I am holding below the verified bar.

Sequichie Comingdeer was a real Cherokee teacher and author, and this line circulates consistently under his name in inspirational collections. I cannot place it in any book, lecture, or documented interview, and quotations attributed to Native American teachers are unusually prone to unsourced circulation and invented attribution. Attribution is uncontested but unsupported by anything I can point to.

Consistent with Shakti Gawain's published voice and themes, and attributed to her without competition. Most likely from Living in the Light (1986) or an interview, but I cannot place it, and this is generic enough New Age phrasing that I would not bet on the specific book. No citation asserted.

Distinctively Gawain in content — the doubting-and-contradicting-intuition observation is a central argument of Living in the Light (1986), and I believe the line comes from that book, but I cannot confirm the chapter or exact page from memory and so am not asserting the citation. Attribution to Gawain is strong on internal evidence; the print source is unestablished.

Attributed consistently to Shakti Gawain and consistent with her work on light, shadow, and non-resistance. The shadow-and-light image itself is ancient and appears in many traditions, so the metaphor is not evidence of authorship — only this particular formulation would be. I cannot place the formulation in a specific Gawain title. Note the text carries a bracketed editorial fix ('stomp[ing]'), suggesting it was transcribed from a secondary source rather than a book.

Subject matter points to Creating True Prosperity (1997), Gawain's book specifically about money and abundance, and the framing of money as a mirror of internal process is that book's core thesis. I cannot confirm the sentence appears there verbatim, so I am not asserting the citation. Attribution to Gawain is plausible and uncontested.

The relationships-as-mirror teaching is a signature Gawain theme, developed at length in Living in the Light (1986), and the passage reads like continuous prose from a book rather than a manufactured aphorism — the internal ellipsis suggests it was excerpted from a longer paragraph. Attribution is credible on internal evidence; I cannot verify the source, so no citation is asserted.

This is attributed to Shalom Ormsby, the owner and maintainer of this corpus, and appears to be an original line rather than a quotation from any published source. I have no training knowledge of it, which is the expected result for an unpublished original and is not evidence against it. My tooling cannot validate first-party authorship, so the low confidence here reflects the limits of my method, not doubt about the claim. This one should be settled by human confirmation at review time rather than by provenance research; if the author confirms it, it can be promoted directly.

Sherrill Sellman is a real author in the natural-health field (Hormone Heresy and related titles), and the body-as-barometer framing fits that domain. I cannot place the quote in any of her books or articles, and it circulates mainly through wellness quote collections, which are a low-reliability chain. Plausible, unsourced.

Shirley Hufstedler — federal appellate judge and the first U.S. Secretary of Education — is consistently named as the source, and the line appears in compilations of quotations by American women, likely originating in an interview or speech. That kind of origin is real but hard to verify, and I cannot identify the occasion or publication. Attribution is stable across sources but rests on repetition rather than documentation.

results.earliest_print_source: Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, Shunryu Suzuki, Weatherhill, 1970 (Prologue)
results.notes: The single most famous line in the book, from the Prologue titled 'Beginner's Mind.' One wording note: the original reads 'but in the expert's there are few' — the corpus text adds a second 'mind' ('in the expert's mind there are few'). It is a common and harmless variant, but if the corpus aims at exact quotation the shorter form is the published one.

results.earliest_print_source: Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, Shunryu Suzuki, Weatherhill, 1970
results.notes: Genuine Suzuki from Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind; I recall it from the 'Right Practice / Right Attitude' material but cannot pin the exact chapter. The published wording is 'Zen is not some kind of excitement, but concentration on our usual everyday routine' — the corpus text inserts 'merely' before 'concentration.' Minor variant worth normalizing.

results.earliest_print_source: Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, Shunryu Suzuki, Weatherhill, 1970
results.notes: I recall this as the closing sentence of Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, in the final section on Zen mind, and the wording is short and exact enough that it is unlikely to be a paraphrase. Confidence is held at 0.80 rather than higher because I am relying on recall of placement within the book rather than a checked page.

Consistently attributed to Shunryu Suzuki and characteristic of his teaching, likely from Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind or the later collection Not Always So. I cannot place it in either with enough confidence to name the book, so the print source is left null. Below the promotion bar on sourcing, not on plausibility.

Sidney Madwed was a real motivational speaker and poet whose lines circulate widely on aggregator sites, and this one is consistently attributed to him, but I cannot place it in any book, article, or speech transcript I know of. The claim itself ('the subconscious cannot tell the difference between reality and imagination') is a stock New Thought / self-help proposition that predates Madwed by decades, so he may be restating rather than originating it. No citation available.

The idea is genuinely Freud's: he described thinking as 'Probehandeln' — trial or experimental action — notably in 'Formulations on the Two Principles of Mental Functioning' (1911), where thought is characterized as experimental action carried out with small quantities of energy, and again in later work. 'Thought is action in rehearsal' is a compressed English aphorism of that concept rather than any translator's rendering I can point to in the Standard Edition. Attribution to Freud is sound at the level of idea; the exact wording is popularizer's phrasing, so I am holding this below the promotion bar.

results.earliest_print_source: The Hound of the Baskervilles, Arthur Conan Doyle, 1902
results.notes: Spoken by Sherlock Holmes in 'The Hound of the Baskervilles' (1902), early in the novel. The canonical wording is 'The world is full of obvious things which nobody by any chance ever observes' — the corpus text substitutes 'notices' for 'observes' and inserts a comma. Recommend restoring the published wording. Note also that this is a fictional character's line, not Conan Doyle speaking in his own voice.

results.earliest_print_source: Memoirs of the Life, Writings, and Discoveries of Sir Isaac Newton, David Brewster, 1855
results.notes: Newton's seashore remark is well documented, but the corpus text is a loose paraphrase, not the recorded wording. The standard version: 'I do not know what I may appear to the world, but to myself I seem to have been only like a boy playing on the sea-shore, and diverting myself in now and then finding a smoother pebble or a prettier shell than ordinary, whilst the great ocean of truth lay all undiscovered before me.' Recorded by Joseph Spence (Anecdotes, collected in Newton's lifetime, published 1820) and given wide currency by Brewster's 1855 Memoirs. 'Searching for an ever more perfect pebble or seashell' is a modern rewrite. High confidence Newton said something very close to this; low confidence in this specific text, hence attributed rather than verified. Strongly recommend replacing with the canonical wording.

Consistently attributed to Sir John Lubbock (Lord Avebury) across quotation collections, and it is stylistically at home in his popular essay collections 'The Pleasures of Life' (1887) and 'The Use of Life' (1894). I believe it comes from one of those two, but I cannot state which with confidence, so I am not citing a source. Lubbock is not a misattribution magnet and the attribution is stable, which supports a moderate rating; the missing citation keeps it below the bar.

results.earliest_print_source: "Do Schools Kill Creativity?", TED talk, Ken Robinson, February 2006
results.notes: A well-known line from Robinson's February 2006 TED talk 'Do Schools Kill Creativity?', in the passage arguing that children will take a chance and are not frightened of being wrong. The same argument appears in his book 'Out of Our Minds: Learning to Be Creative'. Wording in the talk is 'If you're not prepared to be wrong, you'll never come up with anything original' — matches the corpus text.

Churchill is a documented misattribution magnet and this line has no primary source I can identify in his speeches, books, or letters. It circulates in two forms: 'Men occasionally stumble over the truth...' (the older form, found in mid-20th-century Churchill anecdote compilations) and the later gender-neutral 'Everyone stumbles...' variant used here. Churchill quotation scholarship treats sayings of this kind that surface only in compiled anecdote books with suspicion. Plausible but unconfirmed; the corpus text is in any case the later rewritten variant, not the earliest attributed form.

results.earliest_print_source: The Examiner, No. 14, Jonathan Swift, 1710
results.notes: The Churchill attribution is spurious. This is a modern variant of a saying with a long documented pedigree: Jonathan Swift wrote 'Falsehood flies, and the Truth comes limping after it' in The Examiner (1710), and the 'boots' form — 'A lie will go round the world while truth is pulling its boots on' — circulated in the 19th century, commonly credited to the preacher C. H. Spurgeon, who himself presented it as an old saying. 'Pants on' is a 20th-century Americanized rewrite. Versions of this line are also misattributed to Mark Twain, another magnet. There is no evidence Churchill originated it.
results.suggested_reattribution: Jonathan Swift (1710, earliest documented form); the 'boots' variant is commonly credited to C. H. Spurgeon in the 19th century

results.earliest_print_source: The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying, Sogyal Rinpoche, 1992
results.notes: The two-selves passage — the garrulous, demanding, hysterical, calculating ego versus the hidden spiritual being whose still voice of wisdom is rarely heard — is characteristic of and, to my knowledge, drawn from 'The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying' (1992). I am confident about the book but not about chapter or page, and the corpus text appears spliced: the closing clause ('you have uncovered in yourself your own wise guide') does not grammatically follow the preceding sentence and looks like material lifted from further down the same passage. Recommend re-checking against the book and repairing the ellipsis before promotion.

I know of nothing in Kierkegaard's authorship resembling this, in any standard translation. The diction is modern therapeutic/mindfulness aphorism — the Gestalt 'paradoxical theory of change' register — not Kierkegaard's, whose treatment of becoming is far more elaborated and anguished. It reads like a coaching-literature line that acquired a prestigious name. I cannot identify the real originator, so I am not proposing a reattribution, but I would not promote this under Kierkegaard's name.

results.earliest_print_source: Either/Or, Part I, "Diapsalmata", Søren Kierkegaard, 1843
results.notes: Genuine Kierkegaard, from the 'Diapsalmata' aphorisms opening Either/Or Part I (1843), written in the voice of the aesthete 'A'. Familiar in both the Swenson and Hong translations. The original aphorism continues '...For pleasure disappoints, possibility never' — the corpus text truncates before that clause, which is a legitimate excerpt rather than a distortion. Note for the record that the speaker is a pseudonymous persona, as with most of Kierkegaard's aesthetic writing.

results.earliest_print_source: The Mother, Sri Aurobindo, 1928
results.notes: This is the opening of the well-known passage on money in Sri Aurobindo's short book 'The Mother' (1928), in the section treating money as one of the powers to be conquered and returned to the Divine. The wording matches the standard Sri Aurobindo Ashram edition as I know it. Confident in book and passage; slightly short of 0.9 only because I cannot confirm the section numbering.

Self-transcendence and 'competing only with yourself' were central, endlessly repeated themes of Sri Chinmoy's talks and writings, and the vocabulary here is authentically his. But he published hundreds of volumes of aphorisms and transcribed lectures, and I cannot locate this specific text in any of them; the ellipsis suggests it has been assembled from more than one sentence. Attribution is plausible and stylistically consistent, but uncited.

Anachronistic. 'Unconditional self acceptance' is a term of art from Albert Ellis's Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy, and the whole passage — separating mistakes from intrinsic worth, 'a peaceful mind' — is 20th-century cognitive-therapy and self-esteem language with no counterpart in the devotional writing of a 17th-century bishop. Francis de Sales wrote about gentleness toward one's own faults, which is probably why his name attached itself here, but his framing is theological (worth grounded in God), not psychological. I cannot identify who actually wrote this, so I am proposing no reattribution; Ellis is the likely conceptual source rather than a confirmed author.

This one is genuinely at home in Francis de Sales: gentleness in the face of difficulty, and the counsel to bend rather than break, are signatures of his spiritual direction in 'Introduction to the Devout Life' and his letters. It appears in Catholic devotional compilations of his sayings, usually paired with 'Do not lose your inner peace for anything whatsoever.' I cannot pin it to a specific letter or chapter, and translation-era English makes exact matching hard, so no citation. Moderate confidence, unlike q_1292 which I judge to be a modern fabrication under the same name.

This belongs to the same apocryphal cluster as 'Preach the Gospel at all times; when necessary, use words' — a line Franciscan scholars have repeatedly shown is absent from Francis's writings and from the early biographies. The 'walking is our preaching' version derives from a later retelling of an anecdote about Francis walking through town with a companion, and appears in modern devotional literature rather than in any source contemporary with him. Not found in the Writings of Francis or in Celano/Bonaventure as far as I know.

No evidence connects this to Francis of Assisi. It does not appear in his authenticated writings or in the early Franciscan biographies, and the earliest instances I am aware of are 20th-century, in motivational and recovery literature, where it circulated for some time before Francis's name was attached. The rhetorical shape — necessary, possible, impossible — is a modern three-beat inspirational construction. Widely repeated, which is not evidence.

Stanley Horowitz is a real and otherwise obscure figure best known for a Reader's Digest contest-winning line about the seasons ('Winter is an etching, spring a watercolor...'). This aphorism is consistently credited to him in quotation collections, which suggests a shared original source — plausibly the same magazine-filler context — but I cannot identify a publication or date. Attribution is stable but entirely uncited.

Consistent with Covey's Habit 1 material on proactivity and the freedom to choose one's response, which he built explicitly on Viktor Frankl. The sentiment is authentically his and the attribution is stable, but I cannot place this exact sentence in 'The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People' (1989) or 'Principle-Centered Leadership' (1991), and Covey also said versions of this in many talks. Note the underlying idea traces to Frankl, not Covey.

Stephen Larsen is a real author — Joseph Campbell's biographer, with Robin Larsen, of 'A Fire in the Mind' — and this passage is written in a Campbellian register, which is precisely the problem: 'say yes to life even though you know it will devour you' echoes Campbell's affirmation-of-life and 'joyful participation in the sorrows of the world' themes closely enough that the two men's names could easily have been swapped in transmission. I cannot place the text in Larsen's own books, nor confirm it as a Campbell quotation. Uncertain enough that I am proposing no reattribution.

Authentically Levine in vocabulary and cadence — 'letting go', meeting oneself anew, healing as distinct from curing are the core of his work with the dying. Most likely from 'Healing into Life and Death' (1987) or 'Who Dies?' (1982), but I cannot confirm which, so no citation. Attribution stable across sources and stylistically sound; uncited.

Same assessment as q_1299: the framing — that becoming loving is subtractive, a letting go of accreted self-concept rather than an achievement — is a recognizable Stephen Levine teaching, and the attribution is consistent wherever it appears. I cannot identify the book. Uncited, and the opening sentence's grammar ('People ask what must they become') suggests transcription from a talk rather than from print.

The four human endowments — self-awareness, conscience, independent will, creative imagination — are a genuine and distinctive Covey framework, presented in 'The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People' (1989) and developed further in 'Principle-Centered Leadership' (1991). Attribution to Covey is not in doubt. The circulating text, with its ellipsis, is a condensation rather than a verbatim sentence from either book, which is why I am not citing a page or crossing the promotion bar. Note this is the same author as q_1297, entered under a different name form ('Stephen Covey' vs 'Stephen R. Covey') — worth normalizing in the corpus.

Sounds like Covey speaking rather than writing — the direct second-person challenge and the appeal to 'universal principles' are his, but the loose, spoken syntax points to a seminar or interview rather than a book. I cannot place it in any of his published works. Plausible, uncited.

Steve DeMasco is a real figure — Shaolin martial artist and author of 'The Shaolin Way' (2006) — and this line is consistently credited to him, plausibly from that book or from an interview around its publication. I cannot confirm the source. The quote is generic enough that stable attribution carries little evidential weight on its own.

results.earliest_print_source: First Things First, Stephen R. Covey with A. Roger Merrill and Rebecca R. Merrill, 1994
results.notes: The clock/compass framing is the organizing metaphor of the opening of First Things First (1994): the clock stands for commitments, schedules and how we spend time; the compass for vision, values and what matters most; and Covey names the gap between them. This wording is a condensed rendering of that passage rather than a verbatim sentence I can pin to a page, so I withhold the top of the scale. The author name in the record is misspelled: it is Stephen R. Covey, not Steven Covey.

The voice is strongly consistent with Stuart Wilde (1946-2013) — the irreverent register, the ego-as-taskmaster conceit, the closing 'I wouldn't stand for that BS if I were you' — and the line circulates consistently under his name. It plausibly comes from Infinite Self (1996) or Silent Power, but I cannot place it in a specific book or page from training knowledge, so I will not name one.

Circulates widely as an unsourced 'Sufi saying' or 'Sufi epigram' in English-language quotation collections. I know of no Sufi primary text, named poet, or translator behind it, and the polished English antithesis (heart grieves / spirit rejoices) reads like a modern anthology formulation. Generic tradition labels of this kind are effectively unverifiable.

I have no knowledge of Sukh Chugh as a published author, and no recollection of this passage in any book, essay, or collection. The prose reads like contemporary personal-blog or social-media writing. Attribution may well be correct, but I have nothing to confirm it against.

Swami Amar Jyoti (1928-2001), founder of Truth Consciousness, published satsang discourses (Spirit of Himalaya, Retreat Into Eternity) and the line is idiomatically plausible for that body of work. I cannot place it in any specific discourse or volume, and it does not appear in quotation references I can recall.

Genuinely Vivekananda in substance and idiom; 'We are what our thoughts have made us' is a recurring formulation of his and the passage is consistently cited to the Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda. I cannot confirm the volume, lecture, or page from training knowledge, so I leave the print source blank rather than guess a locator. Held below the promotion bar for that reason.

Usually labeled a Swedish proverb in English collections, sometimes simply 'proverb'. I know of no traceable earliest appearance, no Swedish original I can cite, and no scholarly proverb reference that dates it. An honest 'unknown'.

results.earliest_print_source: Self-Help, Samuel Smiles, 1859 (quoting the Rev. Richard Cecil)
results.notes: 'Sydney Smiles' is not a person; this is a corruption of Samuel Smiles, the Scottish author of Self-Help (1859). In Self-Help, Smiles quotes the maxim from the Rev. Richard Cecil, whose usual wording is 'The shortest way to do many things is to do only one thing at once' — so even under the corrected name Smiles is the transmitter, not the author. My recollection of the Self-Help citation is good but not page-level; the confidence figure reflects the weakness of the attribution as recorded, not of the reattribution.
results.suggested_reattribution: Richard Cecil, as quoted by Samuel Smiles in Self-Help (1859)

results.earliest_print_source: Phrynette Married, Marthe Troly-Curtin, 1912
results.notes: A well-documented misattribution. Eliot never wrote this; it appears in Marthe Troly-Curtin's novel Phrynette Married (1912) as 'Time you enjoy wasting is not wasted time', and Quote Investigator traced it there. Wikiquote lists it in the misattributed section of the Eliot page. Low confidence here reflects the near-certainty that the recorded attribution to Eliot is wrong.

results.earliest_print_source: Preface to Transit of Venus: Poems by Harry Crosby, T. S. Eliot, 1931
results.notes: Genuine Eliot. The line comes from his preface to Harry Crosby's posthumous collection Transit of Venus (Black Sun Press, 1931), and Wikiquote carries it as sourced. I am confident in the work and year but have not verified the exact wording against the preface, so I stop short of 'verified'.

results.earliest_print_source: Dante, T. S. Eliot, 1929 (reprinted in Selected Essays, 1932)
results.notes: Genuine and well-sourced Eliot, from his 1929 monograph Dante, which was collected in Selected Essays. The sentence is quoted verbatim in the standard references and the wording in the record matches.

results.earliest_print_source: The Sacred Wood: Essays on Poetry and Criticism, T. S. Eliot, 1920 ('Philip Massinger')
results.notes: Genuine Eliot, from the essay 'Philip Massinger' in The Sacred Wood (1920). The record quotes only the opening clause; the full sentence continues '...bad poets deface what they take, and good poets make it into something better, or at least something different.' Truncation is standard in quotation but worth noting, since the fuller line reverses the cynical reading the short version invites.

results.earliest_print_source: Seven Pillars of Wisdom, T. E. Lawrence, 1926 (introductory chapter)
results.notes: The author field is wrong by one initial: this is T. E. Lawrence (Lawrence of Arabia), not T. S. Lawrence — almost certainly contaminated by the neighbouring T. S. Eliot entries. The passage is from the introductory chapter of Seven Pillars of Wisdom (1926) and the wording in the record matches the standard text.

Consistently attributed to Tarthang Tulku in quotation collections and idiomatically consistent with his Dharma Publishing books (Skillful Means, Gesture of Balance, Knowledge of Freedom). I cannot locate it in a specific book or chapter, so no print source is offered.

Same situation as the preceding Tarthang Tulku line: plausible in voice and consistently attributed to him in secondary collections, but I can place it in no specific work. Slightly weaker than q_1319 because it circulates less and the phrasing is more generic.

Authentically Teilhardian in both doctrine and phrasing — love as the physical energy that draws fragments toward convergence is central to his cosmology — and the line is consistently attributed to him. However, sources differ on the work (variously The Phenomenon of Man, Human Energy, and the essays collected in Toward the Future), and I cannot resolve which is correct or confirm the translation, so I name no source. Full name is Pierre Teilhard de Chardin.

Terri Guillemets is a contemporary American quotation anthologist (The Quote Garden) who also writes original aphorisms, and this is one of hers rather than an anonymous line she collected. Attribution is consistent wherever it appears. Original publication is self-published online rather than in print, so there is no print source to cite and no independent scholarly confirmation.

results.earliest_print_source: Apologeticus (The Apology), Tertullian, c. 197 AD, ch. 9
results.notes: Genuine Tertullian, rendering 'etiam fructus omnis iam in semine est' from Apologeticus ch. 9. Important context: it is not a general aphorism about potential — Tertullian is arguing against abortion ('he is a man who is going to be one; the whole fruit is already present in the seed'). Anyone using the line as a standalone metaphor should know the argument it belongs to. Confidence held at 0.8 because I am recalling the chapter from memory of the Latin, not verifying an edition.

results.earliest_print_source: The Book of Job 12:8, King James Version, 1611
results.notes: Accurate KJV text. The full verse reads 'Or speak to the earth, and it shall teach thee: and the fishes of the sea shall declare unto thee.' Citation in the record (Job 12:8) is correct; the quoted fragment is the first clause.

The sentence is idiomatically ACIM — wholeness, lack, and demand are its standard vocabulary — and it is consistently attributed to the Course. But ACIM is a large text with a precise numbering system (T-/W-/M- locators), and I cannot place this line at any chapter or section. Without a locator I will not assert the source. Also note the title is A Course in Miracles, not 'The Course in Miracles'.

This is an item from the chain-circulated list 'Instructions for Life in the New Millennium', which spread by email in the late 1990s under the Dalai Lama's name. The Office of the Dalai Lama has disclaimed the list; it is not his, and several of its items track secular American self-help writing (H. Jackson Brown Jr.'s Life's Little Instruction Book is often noted as a source of similar material). Wikiquote treats the list as misattributed. I cannot identify the actual author of this specific line, so I offer no reattribution. A classic misattribution magnet — treat any bare 'Dalai Lama' aphorism in this register with suspicion.

results.earliest_print_source: Gospel of Thomas, saying 70 (Nag Hammadi Codex II, c. 2nd century CE); English in The Nag Hammadi Library in English, ed. James M. Robinson, 1977
results.notes: Saying 70 of the Coptic Gospel of Thomas, recovered at Nag Hammadi in 1945. The Coptic is damaged and translations vary considerably — several render it 'That which you have will save you if you bring it forth from yourselves; that which you do not have within you will kill you if you do not have it within you.' The elegant parallel wording in the record is one translation tradition (popularized via Elaine Pagels and Joseph Campbell), not the only one. The attribution to the text is solid; the exact English is translator-dependent.

results.earliest_print_source: Isha Upanishad 6-7; this English rendering from The Ten Principal Upanishads, trans. Shree Purohit Swami and W. B. Yeats, 1937
results.notes: The source text is certain: Isha Upanishad verses 6-7, on seeing all beings in the Self and the Self in all beings, therefore knowing no hatred or sorrow. The distinctive English phrasing ('Of a certainty...') I believe is the Purohit Swami/Yeats translation rather than Mascaro or Radhakrishnan; I am confident enough to name it but flag it as a translation identification, not a verified collation. The author field would be more precise as 'Isha Upanishad' than the general 'Upanishads'.

I know of no Vedic passage corresponding to this, in any standard translation. The epigram's shape — a chiasmus about using memory rather than being used by it — is a modern rhetorical form, and 'The Vedas' is exactly the kind of blanket ancient-authority label that gets attached to unsourced aphorisms. Very likely modern and pseudo-attributed, but since I cannot name a real author I am not calling it a misattribution outright.

Consistently attributed to the poet Theodore Roethke (1908-1963) across quotation collections, with no competing claimant that I know of. It most likely comes from his notebooks rather than the published poems — Straw for the Fire: From the Notebooks of Theodore Roethke (ed. David Wagoner, 1972) is the usual candidate — but I cannot confirm that, so I name no source. Consistent attribution without a locatable text keeps this below the promotion bar.

Circulates widely in motivational compilations as Theodore Roosevelt, but I cannot place it in any of his speeches, letters, or books that I know. The colloquial 'tell 'em' phrasing is the kind of line that gets retrofitted onto TR as a can-do figurehead. No primary source known to me; honest answer is that the attribution is unsupported rather than disproven.

Consistently and specifically attributed to Theodore Isaac Rubin, the American psychiatrist and author (1923-2019), across self-help and psychology anthologies. The construction and content match his popular writing on emotional life. I cannot identify which of his books it comes from, so no print citation. Note the corpus author field reads 'Theodore Rubin' — the full form 'Theodore Isaac Rubin' is the standard one and would reduce confusion with other Rubins.

This is a composite paraphrase, not a verbatim Thich Nhat Hanh passage. Two authentic teachings of his are welded together here: the walking-on-water line from The Miracle of Mindfulness (1975), which runs roughly 'People usually consider walking on water or in thin air a miracle. But I think the real miracle is not to walk either on water or in thin air, but to walk on earth'; and the 'walk as if you are kissing the Earth with your feet' instruction associated with Peace Is Every Step (1991). The closing sentences about 'our presence alone is a miracle' and saying 'Yes' to the miracles of life I cannot place in his work at all. The corpus author field 'Inspired by Thich Nhat Hanh's teachings' is accurate framing, and the text should not be presented as a direct quotation.

I cannot place this in Thich Nhat Hanh's writing, and the vocabulary is off for him — 'closer to your spirit or further away from it' is Western self-development diction, not the mindfulness/interbeing register he actually uses (he would speak of mindfulness, breath, the present moment, not 'your spirit'). Reads like a social-media caption that acquired a monk's name. No traceable source; no candidate true author identifiable, so no reattribution offered.
