Short, generic sentence widely circulated under Thich Nhat Hanh's name. The thought — that each moment holds more possibility than we notice — is consonant with his teaching, but the line is brief and unmarked enough that I cannot distinguish an authentic sentence from a paraphrase of one. No book, talk, or page reference known to me.

The teaching is unmistakably Thich Nhat Hanh's — seeing clouds, sunshine, minerals, and time inside a single object is his signature illustration of interbeing, developed at length in The Heart of Understanding (1988), his commentary on the Heart Sutra, where the same move is made with a sheet of paper ('If you are a poet, you will see clearly that there is a cloud floating in this sheet of paper'). The flower variant appears across his talks. What I cannot confirm is that this exact wording is his rather than a paraphrase by an editor or reader, so I am holding below the promotion bar. Also note a transcription error in the corpus text: 'Without clouds that could be no rain' should read 'there could be no rain'.

Consistent with Thich Nhat Hanh's recurring teaching that personal peace propagates outward to family and society — a theme carried through Being Peace (1987) and Peace Is Every Step (1991). I cannot confirm this specific sentence as his wording versus a summary of the teaching. No page-level source known to me.

Consistently attributed to Thomas Carlyle in nineteenth- and twentieth-century quotation dictionaries, usually in the form 'Let him who would move and convince others, be first moved and convinced himself.' The sentiment and the periodic sentence structure fit Carlyle's essayistic prose. I cannot identify the specific essay or volume, so no print citation; the attribution itself is old and stable, which is why this sits at 'attributed' rather than lower.

Thomas D. Willhite (1940-1983) founded PSI Seminars, and this passage circulates within that human-potential lineage and its derivative literature, always under his name. The pendulum metaphor and the 'sit still in neutral' line match the seminar idiom of that world. Attribution is consistent but narrow — I know of no independent published source, and material from seminar transcripts is hard to verify. No citation offered.

One of the most-repeated Edison lines and one of the least documented. It does not appear in his notebooks or documented interviews as far as I know, and my recollection of the quotation-research literature is that attributions to Edison cluster well after his death in 1931, with earlier anonymous 'opportunity in overalls' sayings in circulation before his name attached to any of them. I do not have a confident earliest instance or a true author, so I am not calling it misattributed outright — but treat the Edison attribution as unsupported.

Widely repeated as Edison, commonly in the variant 'If we did all the things we are capable of, we would literally astound ourselves.' I cannot place it in any of his writings, interviews, or authorized biographies. Edison is a strong misattribution magnet for terse work-ethic aphorisms. No source, no alternative author known to me.

Attributed to Thomas Fuller, and the form is exactly that of the numbered maxims in Gnomologia: Adagies and Proverbs (1732), compiled by Thomas Fuller, M.D. (1654-1734) — as distinct from the earlier churchman Thomas Fuller (1608-1661), with whom he is routinely confused in quote collections. I could not confirm this specific maxim in Gnomologia from memory, so I am not asserting that citation. Also worth flagging: Gnomologia is a compilation of existing proverbs, so even a confirmed entry would make Fuller the collector rather than the author.

This 'breaks the bridge over which he must pass himself' saying has a genuinely contested attribution: it appears in quotation dictionaries under Thomas Fuller and also under Edward Herbert, Lord Herbert of Cherbury (1583-1648), and I have seen it credited to George Herbert as well. I do not know which is earliest and cannot resolve the tangle from memory, so no reattribution is offered — but the Fuller attribution here should not be treated as settled.

Attributed to Thomas J. Watson Sr., the IBM founder, in business and leadership anthologies. Watson Sr. did speak and write extensively on conduct and courtesy as company doctrine, so the sentiment is in character, but I cannot tie this wording to a speech, a THINK-era publication, or any IBM document. Note also that Watson Sr. and his son Watson Jr. are frequently conflated in quote collections (see q_1354 in this same batch).

The Jefferson attribution is almost certainly wrong. To my knowledge this line appears on the Jefferson Monticello foundation's list of spurious quotations — it is not found anywhere in his correspondence or published writings, and the idiom is twentieth-century American rather than eighteenth-century. It is also commonly credited to Franklin D. Roosevelt, which is itself unverified. Best current understanding is an anonymous early-twentieth-century saying that later collected famous names; because I cannot name the real originator with confidence, I am leaving the reattribution field null rather than guessing FDR.

Not Jefferson. This is a documented spurious Jefferson quotation — it does not appear in his writings, and the Monticello foundation lists it among quotes wrongly ascribed to him. My recollection of Quote Investigator's research is that the earliest located version belongs to Coleman Cox, an American aphorist writing in the early 1920s, in the form 'I am a great believer in Luck. The harder I work, the more of it I seem to have'; the saying was later also pinned on Stephen Leacock and Samuel Goldwyn. I am naming Cox as the probable originator on the strength of that research but deliberately leaving earliest_print_source null, since I cannot confirm the exact volume and year without looking it up.

A well-known formulation from Fr. Thomas Keating (1923-2018), the Trappist monk who developed Centering Prayer. The distinction between effort and consent is load-bearing in his method — consent to God's presence and action is the definitional move of Centering Prayer — and this sentence is quoted consistently under his name throughout contemplative literature. I cannot pin it to Open Mind, Open Heart, Invitation to Love, or a specific conference talk, so no print citation.

Attributed consistently to Thomas J. Leonard (1955-2003), the founder of Coach U and a principal architect of the professional coaching field. The motivation/inspiration contrast is a standard piece of his teaching and the wording is stable across coaching sources. I cannot connect it to The Portable Coach, his newsletters, or any dated publication, so the attribution stays unverified.

Strongly characteristic of Thomas Moore, the Jungian-influenced former monk who wrote Care of the Soul (1992). The argument — that heroic productivity is a real good but a different good from what the soul needs, and that soul wants reverie, beauty, relatedness, and rhythm — is the central thesis of that book and recurs in The Re-Enchantment of Everyday Life (1996). I believe this is authentic Moore prose rather than a paraphrase, but I cannot identify which book or page, so no citation and no promotion above the bar.

Reads as spoken rather than written — the hedged opening ('I think we would be able to') suggests an interview or lecture transcript, and it is attributed to Thomas Moore in that form. The content matches his argument for a spirituality of the immediate and ordinary over an abstract or transcendent one. Without a named interview or program I cannot verify it.

Consistent with Thomas Moore's writing on friendship and intimacy, the territory of Soul Mates: Honoring the Mysteries of Love and Relationship (1994), and attributed to him wherever I have encountered it. The concessive move ('may seem like such a simple, obvious suggestion, but') is his rhetorical habit. No specific source identifiable, so unverified.

Long and stably attributed to Thomas Paine, and the compressed antithesis is genuinely in his rhetorical style. It is usually cited to The American Crisis series (1776-1783), which I believe is correct, but I cannot confirm which number in the series and will not guess at one. Holding at 'attributed' on the strength of the consistent historical attribution rather than a located passage.

This is a genuine and well-documented Watson Jr. formulation, not a floating aphorism. As IBM CEO he made design a corporate program — bringing in Eliot Noyes, and through him Paul Rand and Charles Eames — and 'good design is good business' was his standing argument for it, delivered as the title of a lecture he gave at the Wharton School in the early 1970s and repeated throughout IBM's design literature. The attribution is treated as settled in design history. I am confident of the phrase and the speaker; I am not certain enough of the exact lecture date or published venue to state a formal citation, so earliest_print_source is left null. Author field is correct as Thomas Watson Jr. (distinct from his father, q_1345).

results.earliest_print_source: Walden; or, Life in the Woods, Henry David Thoreau, 1854 (chapter 1, 'Economy')
results.notes: Authentic Thoreau, from the 'Economy' chapter of Walden. The canonical wording is 'In the long run men hit only what they aim at. Therefore, though they should fail immediately, they had better aim at something high.' The corpus text has been silently modernized to 'we only hit what we aim at' — it preserves the meaning but is not what Thoreau wrote, and the second sentence, which carries the point, has been dropped. Recommend restoring the original wording before publication; the verdict is high-confidence on the source, with the caveat that the quoted text is a paraphrase of it.

Genuine Thornton Wilder, and among his most-quoted lines. My recollection places it in the novel The Woman of Andros (1930), spoken in the reflective register of that book rather than in Our Town, to which it is sometimes loosely assigned. Because I am working from memory and cannot confirm the passage, I have left earliest_print_source null rather than state a citation I cannot check — but the Wilder attribution itself is solid and the novel is the likely home.

Extremely widely circulated under Teilhard de Chardin's name (also spelled correctly 'Teilhard'), but I cannot place it in any of his published works (The Divine Milieu, The Phenomenon of Man, Hymn of the Universe, letters). The same line, in French — 'La joie est le signe infaillible de la presence de Dieu' — is commonly credited to the French Catholic writer Leon Bloy, and that attribution appears at least as often in Catholic sources. I am not confident enough in the Bloy origin to reattribute outright, but the Teilhard attribution should not be treated as established.

results.earliest_print_source: "Three Methods of Reform", in Pamphlets: Translated from the Russian, Leo Tolstoy, trans. Aylmer Maude, 1900
results.notes: Genuine Tolstoy. The standard sourced citation is the essay 'Three Methods of Reform' in Aylmer Maude's 1900 translation Pamphlets: Translated from the Russian. Attribution is consistent across reference works and I recall the specific sourced entry rather than only the floating popular version. Author field should be normalized to 'Leo Tolstoy'.

Reads unmistakably like Tom Robbins and is consistently attributed to him, most often to the novel Even Cowgirls Get the Blues (1976). I recall the line in that context but cannot confirm the novel or page with enough certainty to call it verified. No competing attribution exists, which is a point in its favor.

Consistently attributed to Toni Morrison and consistent with her recurring argument that racism imprisons the oppressor as well as the oppressed. It circulates as an interview or lecture remark rather than a passage from her fiction or essays; I cannot identify the specific interview, date, or outlet. No competing attribution. Holding below the promotion bar for lack of a locatable source.

Stylistically and substantively consistent with Tony Hillerman's Navajo Tribal Police novels — it reads as Joe Leaphorn (or Jim Chee) explaining the contrast between petitionary prayer and Navajo restorative ceremony, a theme Hillerman returns to repeatedly. I cannot identify which novel it comes from, and passages of dialogue lifted from novels are frequently reworded in circulation. Plausibly authentic, unverified as to source and exact wording.

Trish Whynot is a contemporary self-help author and holistic counselor; the line is consistent with her published work and I know of no competing attribution, which is typical for quotes from minor contemporary authors — they are rarely misattributed but also rarely sourced. I cannot point to a specific book or page. Low confidence reflects absence of evidence, not suspicion.

Attributed to Truman Capote with unusual consistency across quotation collections, and the aphoristic style fits him. However, it circulates only as a free-floating epigram — I cannot connect it to a specific book, essay, or interview, and Capote's published prose is well indexed, so the absence of a source is a mild concern. Attribution is plausible and uncontested but not evidenced.

'Ts'ai Ken T'an' is not an author — it is the Wade-Giles title of the Caigentan (Vegetable Root Discourse), a late-Ming aphorism collection by Hong Zicheng (Hong Yingming), c. 1590. The saying itself is considerably older than that collection: the Chinese proverb 'shui zhi qing ze wu yu, ren zhi cha ze wu tu' (water too clear has no fish; a person too exacting has no companions) is recorded in Han-dynasty sources, notably Dongfang Shuo's 'Answering a Guest's Objections' as preserved in the Book of Han, and in the Da Dai Liji. So the line is a classical Chinese proverb that the Caigentan may transmit rather than originate. The author field should at minimum be corrected to name Hong Zicheng or be marked as a Chinese proverb.
results.suggested_reattribution: Classical Chinese proverb (Han-era; cf. Dongfang Shuo in the Book of Han) — not original to the Caigentan

results.notes: An anonymous backronym long current in twelve-step recovery culture (Alcoholics Anonymous and related fellowships), where multiple expansions of FEAR circulate — 'False Evidence Appearing Real', 'Face Everything And Recover', 'Forget Everything And Run'. No identifiable originator; it is folk material and correctly listed as Unknown. Zig Ziglar and others popularized it but did not coin it as far as I know.

Usually credited to 'Carl Bard', a figure for whom no biographical record is generally produced — a pattern that often signals an invented or garbled attribution. A near-identical line is credited to Maria Robinson ('Nobody can go back and start a new beginning, but anyone can start today and make a new ending'), equally without a source. 'Unknown' is the honest label; I would not reattribute to either name.

Widely credited to Kobi Yamada, the Compendium author, and it fits the aphoristic gift-book genre he works in; the attribution is common but I have seen no source citation for it. It also circulates freely as an anonymous saying. 'Unknown' is defensible; Yamada is the leading candidate but unconfirmed.

This exact wording ('change the way you think about it') is most often credited to the illustrator Mary Engelbreit, whose artwork popularized it. A closely related and better-sourced line is Maya Angelou's 'If you don't like something, change it. If you can't change it, change your attitude', which appears in her 1993 collection Wouldn't Take Nothing for My Journey Now. The two have cross-contaminated in circulation. Leaving as Unknown is safer than picking one.
I do not recognize this line or any attribution for it. It has the cadence of contemporary leadership or activist writing but I cannot place an author, book, or speech. Honest answer: unknown origin.

This is an English paraphrase of a genuine and much older line by the French writer Alphonse Karr, from Voyage autour de mon jardin (A Tour Round My Garden, 1845): some people grumble that roses have thorns; he is grateful that thorns have roses. The 'I can complain / I can rejoice' rewording is a later inspirational reformulation of unknown authorship, and it is also spuriously attributed to Abraham Lincoln — a classic Lincoln magnet attribution with no basis in his writings. Correctly listed as Unknown for this wording; the underlying thought is Karr's.
results.suggested_reattribution: Paraphrase of Alphonse Karr, Voyage autour de mon jardin (1845); NOT Lincoln

results.notes: Almost always credited to William Arthur Ward, the American inspirational writer, and the attribution is consistent enough to be the leading candidate; Ward's aphorisms are, however, poorly sourced in general and this one circulates without a book or date. A sailing-metaphor variant is also attributed to Ward's contemporaries. Listing as Unknown is acceptable; Ward is the probable author but unverified.

I cannot place this. The dandelion/flower argument about wonder dulled by familiarity is a commonplace found in Chesterton, Emerson, and Carl Sagan among others, but this specific wording does not match any passage I can identify. Unknown origin.

In quotation anthologies this line is generally credited to 'W. B. Prescott', a name that appears attached to it and little else — the kind of thinly documented attribution that anthologies copy from one another. I cannot confirm the person or a print source, so I am not reattributing. Unknown is honest.

Anonymous contemporary inspirational prose in the greeting-card / New Thought register (inner Light, Divine Source). No author, book, or tradition I can identify. Note also that the text carries a stray trailing double quotation mark and a corrupted character (a comma rendered as an encoding artifact after 'no one else'), suggesting it was scraped rather than transcribed from print.

results.earliest_print_source: Thomas Jefferson, letter to Nathaniel Macon, 12 January 1819
results.notes: This is a genuine Thomas Jefferson line, not anonymous. Jefferson wrote 'honesty is the 1st. chapter in the book of wisdom' in a letter to Nathaniel Macon dated 12 January 1819; the Jefferson editorial projects treat it as authentic rather than as one of the many spurious Jefferson quotations. The corpus text also carries a stray leading curly quotation mark that should be stripped. Author should be changed from Unknown to Thomas Jefferson.
Unrecognized. The phrasing has the flavor of a translated Buddhist or Brahma Kumaris 'thought for the day', but I cannot identify a text, teacher, or tradition. Unknown origin.

This is the widely circulated poem usually titled 'Risks'. It is most often credited to Leo Buscaglia, who quoted it in his lectures and books (Living, Loving and Learning), but he was a popularizer rather than the demonstrable author; the poem is also credited to Janet Rand and to William Arthur Ward, and frequently printed as anonymous. Because the competing claims cancel out and none carries a documented first printing that I can confirm, Unknown is the right label. Note the corpus version omits the poem's closing lines about the person who risks nothing.

A comic inversion of the ancient memento mori maxim (compare Marcus Aurelius and Seneca on living each day as if it were the last). The joke form circulates in many phrasings — 'and one day you'll be right', 'and one of these days you will be' — attributed variously to Jerry Rubin, Benny Hill, and others, none of which I can substantiate. Almost certainly a folk witticism with no fixed author.

Closely tracks a genuine Eric Hoffer aphorism — 'You can never get enough of what you don't really want' / 'what you don't need to make you happy' — which appears in his aphoristic writings and is consistently credited to him. The wording here ('what you don't really need') is a common variant that also circulates anonymously and in recovery and simple-living literature. Hoffer is the probable ultimate source, but the exact wording given is not his, so I am not reattributing.

Unrecognized. The sentiment 'there are no winners in war, only survivors' is a widespread commonplace with no single origin; the full sentence with the 'every twenty years' framing I cannot place to any author, speech, or novel. Unknown origin.

Unrecognized as a sourced quotation. It is the mirror image of a line associated with George F. Will — that the pleasant thing about being a pessimist is that you are constantly either proven right or pleasantly surprised — which is itself a widely circulated formulation of an older joke. This pessimist's-consolation gag has many anonymous variants; no identifiable author for this wording.

Popularly attributed to Will Rogers, but I know of no instance in his own writing or columns; the Will Rogers attribution appears decades after his 1935 death and quote researchers have treated it as unsupported. Anonymous newspaper-filler versions of the joke circulated in the early 20th century. Keeping the author as 'Unknown' is the honest choice; I cannot name a first printing.

Anonymous modern aphorism circulated widely in business/motivational material and on posters. I have seen it credited to various columnists and speakers, but no attribution I know of is consistent or documented. No traceable origin in my knowledge.

A show-business/startup proverb with many numeric variants ('five years', 'ten years', 'twenty years'). The best-documented relative is Eddie Cantor's line about taking twenty years to become an overnight success, but that is a different sentence and I cannot connect this five-year phrasing to any named author or first printing.
I cannot place this line. It has the register of a late-20th-century artist's statement or interview remark, but no author, work, or date is retrievable from my knowledge. Honest answer: unknown.
No recollection of this line from any author or work. It resembles aphorisms from contemporary creativity writing, but I can offer no attribution and will not guess.

Very widely circulated in Kundalini Yoga / 3HO circles as a saying of Yogi Bhajan (Harbhajan Singh Khalsa), where it appears in lecture transcripts and teaching collections. The attribution is consistent across that community but I cannot cite a specific dated lecture or printed volume, so it stays unverified. The sentiment also echoes older Sikh and Vedantic formulations, which makes an even earlier antecedent plausible.

This reads as an English rendering of a classical Sanskrit verse on the avadhuta / jivanmukta, and it is most often credited to Bhartrihari's Vairagya Shataka; it circulated in English-speaking spiritual circles partly through Ram Dass's use of it. I am reasonably but not firmly confident of the Bhartrihari source and cannot name the verse number or the translator, so the corpus author 'Unknown' is not wrong, merely incomplete.
Unknown to me. Phrasing suggests contemporary coaching or workshop language rather than a published literary source. No attribution offered.

Consistently credited to Pamela Vaull Starr across greeting-card and anthology sources; the attribution is stable and specific enough to be worth recording, but I know of no primary publication, date, or verified biography confirming it. Stays below the promotion bar for that reason.
I cannot place this. It has the cadence of a devotional or pastoral exhortation and circulates in inspirational collections without a stable author. No attribution I can support.
A homophone-play proverb ('know'/'no') of the same family as 'Know Jesus, know peace; no Jesus, no peace.' Anonymous formula, no traceable first author or printing.
One of the modern mock-beatitudes that circulate anonymously; I have seen it credited to several different clergy and humorists with no consistency. No documented origin in my knowledge.

results.earliest_print_source: Isha Upanishad, verses 5-6 (Sanskrit, c. 6th-4th century BCE)
results.notes: This is a genuine Upanishadic passage, not a modern pastiche. 'It moves and it moves not; it is far and it is near; it is within all this and it is outside all this' is Isha Upanishad 5 (tad ejati tan naijati / tad dure tad v antike / tad antar asya sarvasya / tad u sarvasyasya bahyatah), and 'sees all beings in the Self and the Self in all beings' is Isha Upanishad 6. The English wording here is a modern translation; I cannot identify which translator with confidence, so no translator is claimed. Confidence is high for the source text, and the corpus attribution 'Upanishads' is correct.

Plausibly Upanishadic in substance — the closing clause echoes the Isha Upanishad's 'attains immortality / eternal life' (amrtam asnute) and the renunciation formula of Isha 1-2 — but this is a loose, heavily paraphrastic English rendering and I cannot match it to a specific Upanishad or verse. The theistic framing ('God acts through you') suggests a devotional translator's hand rather than a literal one. The generic attribution 'Upanishads' may well be right in spirit; it is not verifiable from what I know.

results.earliest_print_source: The Lathe of Heaven, Ursula K. Le Guin, 1971 (recalled, not confirmed)
results.notes: I recall this line from Le Guin's The Lathe of Heaven, a novel whose whole subject is sanity and a world gone wrong, and the attribution to Le Guin is consistent wherever I have seen it quoted. I am confident it is hers; I am less confident of the exact novel and cannot cite chapter or page, so the source is flagged as recalled. Note also that the corpus spells the surname 'LeGuin' — the correct form is Ursula K. Le Guin.

This is a well-documented misattribution. Le Guin herself denied writing it, stating on her own website that the line was not hers and asking that it stop being credited to her; quote researchers traced the sentence to the mathematics educator Julian F. Fleron, who wrote a close version in his own work before it drifted onto Le Guin. Confidence 0.15 rates the (weak) attribution to Le Guin, not the misattribution finding, which I hold with reasonable strength. Recommend removing Le Guin as author.

Attributed to Le Guin with reasonable consistency in quote collections, and the thought (imagination as both gift and exile) is characteristic of her essays on fantasy. But I cannot place it in a specific novel, essay, or address, and Le Guin is a magnet for plausible-sounding lines she did not write (see q_1397 in this same batch). Holding below the promotion bar until a text can be named.

Almost certainly not Ursula K. Le Guin. The vocabulary is that of academic religious studies — 'the greatest religious problem today', 'expansion of inner awareness', mysticism paired with social action — and Le Guin, a lifelong non-believer who wrote about Taoism in a very different register, is an implausible author. The likeliest explanation is a first-name collision with another Ursula in a quote list; the attribution I associate with this line is Ursula King, the scholar of mysticism and Teilhard de Chardin, whose subject matter matches exactly. I am not confident enough in that to enter it as a reattribution, so the field is left null. Recommend removing the Le Guin attribution regardless.

results.earliest_print_source: The Dispossessed, Ursula K. Le Guin, 1974 (recalled, not confirmed)
results.notes: I recall this as Shevek's line in The Dispossessed — the imagery of a world that is beautiful whole and 'all dirt and rocks' close up fits Anarres and the novel's argument directly, and the diction ('you lose the pattern') is Le Guin's. Confident in the author, reasonably confident in the novel, unable to cite chapter or page from memory, so it is marked attributed rather than verified. Surname in the corpus should be corrected to Le Guin.

results.earliest_print_source: Bryn Mawr Commencement Address (1986), collected in Dancing at the Edge of the World: Thoughts on Words, Women, Places, Ursula K. Le Guin, 1989
results.notes: Genuine and well-sourced: this is the closing movement of Le Guin's 1986 Bryn Mawr College commencement address, one of her best-known pieces, reprinted in Dancing at the Edge of the World (1989). The 'we are volcanoes / new mountains' passage is quoted from that address routinely and correctly. Surname in the corpus should be corrected to Le Guin.

Vernon Howard (1918-1992) was a real and prolific American self-help and inner-work author, and this line is entirely consistent with his idiom and is consistently credited to him. I cannot name which of his many books it comes from, and his corpus is large enough that unattributed paraphrases circulate under his name, so this stays unverified.

Same assessment as q_1402: stable and plausible attribution to Vernon Howard, whose books turn on self-knowledge as the operative power, but no specific title, edition, or year that I can name. Honest verdict is attribution-without-source.

results.earliest_print_source: This Week magazine, 14 August 1960 (attributed to Vernon Law; recalled, not confirmed)
results.notes: The author name in the corpus is garbled. This is Vernon Sanders Law, the Pittsburgh Pirates pitcher and 1960 Cy Young winner — 'Vernon Saunders' appears to be his middle name mistaken for a surname. The saying is credited to him in a 1960 magazine piece and the attribution has been examined and upheld by quote researchers. Confident in the person; the exact publication date is from memory and should be checked before it is printed as fact.

Widely repeated in design writing and exhibition material as a motto of the Milanese architect and designer Vico Magistretti (1920-2006), and it is consistent with how he described his method. I cannot trace it to a specific interview, lecture, or publication, and short designer mottos of this kind are frequently paraphrased in translation from Italian, so the wording may not be his exactly.

results.earliest_print_source: Histoire d'un crime, Victor Hugo (written 1852, published 1877), conclusion: 'On resiste a l'invasion des armees; on ne resiste pas a l'invasion des idees.'
results.notes: Rooted in Hugo but not a translation of him. Hugo's actual sentence, at the close of Histoire d'un crime, is 'One resists the invasion of armies; one does not resist the invasion of ideas.' The familiar English form with 'stronger than all the armies in the world' and 'an idea whose time has come' is a loose 19th-century paraphrase that took on a life of its own in English-language oratory and journalism. Attributing the sentiment to Hugo is fair; presenting this wording as his words is not. Recommend flagging the text as a paraphrase, or replacing it with the accurate translation.

A pun-shaped motivational quip ('fired with enthusiasm' / 'fired with enthusiasm') that circulates almost entirely in sales and management literature. I know of no Lombardi speech, book, or contemporaneous report containing it, and Lombardi died in 1970 while the line appears to spread in business contexts later. Lombardi is a magnet for coach-flavored aphorisms he did not originate. I cannot name the true source, so no reattribution is offered.

Not van Gogh. The vocabulary is anachronistic and un-translatable back into his idiom: 'weekly paycheck' and 'spiritual in calling' belong to modern American self-help prose, not to the 1870s-80s Dutch/French letters to Theo. I cannot recall this passage anywhere in the collected letters, which are exhaustively indexed. It reads like a 20th-century vocation-and-calling passage that acquired a van Gogh byline. I cannot identify the real author, so no reattribution.

results.earliest_print_source: Letter to Theo van Gogh, Cuesmes, summer 1880 (collected in The Letters of Vincent van Gogh)
results.notes: Genuine van Gogh, from the long Cuesmes letter to Theo written in the summer of 1880 during his turn toward art. The familiar rendering is close to the published translations: someone has a great fire in his soul and nobody ever comes to warm themselves at it, and passers-by see only a little smoke at the top of the chimney. Wording varies slightly between translations, but the passage itself is well documented in the letters corpus.

results.earliest_print_source: The Letters of Vincent van Gogh — letter to Theo, 1882
results.notes: Consistently and, as far as I can tell, correctly sourced to the letters to Theo from the Hague period (1882), and it appears in the sourced rather than the unsourced sections of reference collections. It also matches van Gogh's actual argument in those letters about patient accumulation over inspiration. I am confident in the attribution but have not pinned the exact letter number, so I stop short of 'verified'.

One of the most-reproduced van Gogh lines and one of the least supported. I cannot place it in the letters, and my recollection is that reference collections file it as unsourced or disputed rather than citing a letter. Its epigrammatic symmetry is unlike his actual prose, which is discursive. Popular but evidentially empty; treat as unsourced unless a letter citation surfaces.

results.earliest_print_source: A Room of One's Own, Virginia Woolf, 1929
results.notes: Genuine Woolf, from A Room of One's Own (1929), in the passage on how writers are deformed by their sensitivity to criticism and reputation. The wording quoted here matches the published text.

Consistently attributed to Woolf and entirely consonant with her essays on autobiography and biography, but I cannot place the exact essay, diary entry, or letter. Plausible sources include the posthumous essay collections or the autobiographical writings, and I will not name one I cannot confirm. Attribution is likely correct; the citation is missing.

results.earliest_print_source: The Diary of Virginia Woolf (also in A Writer's Diary, ed. Leonard Woolf, 1953) — mid-1920s entry
results.notes: This has the compressed, self-observing cadence of the diary rather than the published essays, and my recollection places it in a mid-1920s diary entry, later reprinted in A Writer's Diary. I am confident about author and genre; I have not pinned the exact date, so I stop short of 'verified'.

results.earliest_print_source: La Bégueule, Voltaire, 1772 (also Dictionnaire philosophique, article 'Art dramatique')
results.notes: Voltaire genuinely wrote 'Le mieux est l'ennemi du bien' — in the verse tale La Bégueule (1772) and in the Dictionnaire philosophique. Two caveats worth carrying: the literal sense is 'the better is the enemy of the good', and Voltaire himself presents it as the saying of an Italian sage ('Il meglio è l'inimico del bene'), so he is transmitting a proverb, not coining it. The English form given here is the standard idiomatic rendering.

results.earliest_print_source: Le Mondain, Voltaire, 1736
results.notes: Condensed from the closing line of Voltaire's poem Le Mondain (1736): 'Le paradis terrestre est où je suis' — the earthly paradise is where I am. The attribution is solid; note that the corpus text drops 'earthly', which slightly shifts the poem's worldly, anti-ascetic joke toward a spiritual reading.

Stone did use and promote this maxim — it is central to Success Through a Positive Mental Attitude (1960, with Napoleon Hill) and to his later books — but the core formula descends from Napoleon Hill's 'every adversity, every failure, every heartache carries with it the seed of an equal or greater benefit' (Think and Grow Rich, 1937). The framing sentence here reads like Stone quoting the maxim rather than coining it. Attribution to Stone is defensible; the underlying idea is Hill's, so I have not pinned a print source for this exact sentence.

results.earliest_print_source: The Summing Up, W. Somerset Maugham, 1938
results.notes: Genuine Maugham, from The Summing Up (1938), in his reflections on literary fame and the people it visits. The sentence structure and the contrarian observation are characteristic and I recall it in that book specifically.

Circulates with competing attributions. The closely parallel 'only the mediocre are always at their best' is widely attributed to Jean Giraudoux, and variants appear under Maugham and other early-20th-century wits. I cannot locate the line in Maugham's own texts. Genuine attribution uncertainty rather than a clear misattribution, so no reattribution is offered.

results.earliest_print_source: 'Miracles', Leaves of Grass, Walt Whitman (poem first published 1856)
results.notes: Genuine Whitman, from the poem 'Miracles' in Leaves of Grass: 'To me every hour of the light and dark is a miracle, / Every cubic inch of space is a miracle.' The quoted text matches the poem apart from line breaks rendered as sentences.

results.earliest_print_source: Preface to Leaves of Grass, Walt Whitman, 1855
results.notes: From the 1855 Preface to Leaves of Grass, in the celebrated series of imperatives ('re-examine all you have been told at school or church or in any book, dismiss whatever insults your own soul'). Note the original reads 'your own soul'; the corpus text drops 'own', a small but real deviation from the printed line.

results.earliest_print_source: 'Song of Myself', section 31, Leaves of Grass, Walt Whitman
results.notes: Genuine Whitman, opening line of section 31 of 'Song of Myself': 'I believe a leaf of grass is no less than the journey-work of the stars.' The corpus text inserts 'that' after 'believe', which is a common quotation variant but not the printed wording.

results.earliest_print_source: 'Song of the Open Road', Leaves of Grass, Walt Whitman (first published 1856)
results.notes: Genuine Whitman, from the late sections of 'Song of the Open Road'. One transcription error to fix: the poem reads 'All parts away for the progress of souls', not 'All parts way'. Line breaks in the corpus text also do not match the poem's lineation.

results.earliest_print_source: 'Song of Myself', section 1, Leaves of Grass, Walt Whitman
results.notes: The idea and the author are certainly Whitman, but the wording is corrupted. The printed line, in section 1 of 'Song of Myself', is 'For every atom belonging to me as good belongs to you' — spoken by the poet to the reader. The corpus version reverses the direction and flattens 'as good belongs' into 'equally belongs'. Recommend replacing with the canonical wording before promotion; confidence is held below the bar because what is in the corpus is not what Whitman wrote.

Consistently attributed to Walter Anderson, the Parade magazine editor and author of self-development books in the 1990s. My best guess is that it comes from The Confidence Course (1997) or a related Parade column, but I cannot confirm which, so I leave the print source null rather than guess a title into the record. Author attribution is probably right; sourcing is thin.

I cannot place this quote or identify which Walter Cooper is meant — the name is shared by several people (a chemist, a broadcaster, others) and none is a figure I associate with devotional or inspirational writing. The prose is generic contemporary spiritual-motivational writing of the kind that circulates in anthologies and newsletters without provenance. Honest answer: unknown.

Walter Starcke was a real New Thought author (The Ultimate Revolution, The Third Appearance, It's All God), and this aphorism is consistent with his subject matter, so the attribution is at least plausible. But I cannot locate the line in any of his books and know it only as a free-floating quotation. Note the sentiment is a commonplace with older analogues (Tillich's 'ultimate concern', among others), which makes independent origination easy and attribution weak.

results.earliest_print_source: On Becoming a Leader, Warren Bennis, 1989
results.notes: I recall this passage distinctly as Bennis, including the parenthetical etymological aside about 'authentic' and 'author' that usually accompanies it, and I place it in On Becoming a Leader (1989), his central statement on self-invention as the ground of leadership. I have not pinned the chapter and cannot rule out one of his later books or an essay reprint, so confidence sits below the verified band.

The diction — 'spreading itself like oil over the troubled sea of thought' — is unmistakably early-19th-century and entirely characteristic of Irving's sketch essays, and the attribution is consistent wherever the line appears. But I cannot pin which collection it comes from (The Sketch Book, Bracebridge Hall, and Wolfert's Roost are all plausible), so I leave the print source null rather than guess a title.

Idiomatically Dyer — the ego-versus-acceptance framing is his standard vocabulary across decades of books and talks — but I cannot locate the sentence in a specific book, and much of what circulates under his name comes from unrecorded lectures or from paraphrase. Plausible author, no source.

The closing phrase 'the journey toward real magic' points strongly to Dyer's Real Magic: Creating Miracles in Everyday Life (1992), and the passage's sequence — hold the miracle in mind, get the vision, suspend disbelief — matches that book's method. That is inference from the title phrase rather than recall of the specific page, so I leave the print source null and hold confidence below the promotion bar.

This motivation/inspiration contrast is a signature Wayne Dyer formulation and matches the central argument of his book Inspiration: Your Ultimate Calling (2006), where he distinguishes 'in-spirit' inspiration from grasping an idea by will. I am confident the idea and phrasing are his, but I cannot confirm the exact wording against a page in that book from memory, so I have not filled in a print source. Wording circulates in several near-variants ('...carries you where you are intended to go').

Genuinely Gretzky's; he used the line in press interviews in the early 1980s and it spread from there. I do not have a reliable memory of the exact first newspaper column and date, so I have left the print source blank rather than guess. NOTE: the author field is misspelled 'Wayne Gretsky' — it should be 'Wayne Gretzky'.

Widely and consistently attributed to Gretzky from the 1980s onward, and he did say it. Important caveat: Gretzky himself repeatedly credited the advice to his father, Walter Gretzky, who coached it into him as a boy ('go to where the puck is going, not where it's been'). So Wayne is the popularizer and speaker; Walter is arguably the originator. Exact wording varies between retellings.

I recall this line as Tom Robbins's, appearing in his novel Still Life with Woodpecker (1980), and it also circulates as a recovery-movement slogan from roughly the same era. The Wayne Dyer attribution appears to be a later quote-site accretion — Dyer used the sentiment in talks, but he is not the source. I am confident enough about the Robbins origin to flag the Dyer attribution as doubtful, but not confident enough to call the reattribution settled.
results.suggested_reattribution: Tom Robbins (probable; Still Life with Woodpecker, 1980 — unconfirmed)

results.notes: Wei Wu Wei (pen name of Terence Gray) wrote exactly this kind of self-cancelling Advaita aphorism across Ask the Awakened, All Else Is Bondage, Open Secret, and Posthumous Pieces, so the attribution is stylistically very plausible. But I cannot place this sentence in a specific book or page, and Wei Wu Wei's phrasings are often paraphrased and compressed when quoted online. Honest verdict: plausible, unverified.

The diction, cadence, and argument are unmistakably Wendell Berry's, and the passage reads as authentic to his late-1960s/1970s essay work (the sensibility of The Long-Legged House, 1969, and The Unsettling of America, 1977). I cannot confirm which essay it comes from with the confidence needed to print a citation, so the source field is left null rather than guessed.

Circulates in est/Landmark-adjacent material and quote compilations credited to Werner Erhard, and the imperative framing fits his idiom. I have no primary source — no transcript, book, or dated talk — and Erhard's aphorisms are heavily paraphrased in secondhand collections. Also note the corpus category is 'humor', which looks like a mis-tag; the line is not comic.

Very widely printed as Will Rogers, but Rogers is a documented misattribution magnet: his enormous body of dated newspaper columns means genuine lines are usually traceable, and this one is not, in my knowledge. No column, broadcast, or contemporaneous printing I can point to. Plausible but unsupported.

This saying floats between several claimants — Will Rogers, Mark Twain, Frank Scully, and later Shirley MacLaine — which is the classic signature of an orphan aphorism that gets adopted by famous names. The Twain version is certainly spurious. I know of no Rogers source, and the multiplicity of claimants argues against him specifically.

Among the more consistently Rogers-attributed lines in this cluster — the small-town parrot-and-gossip image fits his voice and era, and it appears across Rogers collections without competing claimants. Still, I cannot name a column or dated source, so it stays below the verification bar.

This is the proverbial 'first law of holes', which was in circulation as an anonymous saying well before it began being credited to Will Rogers, and it was later popularized in British politics by Denis Healey. Rogers attributions to it appear to be retrofitted. Probable true origin is anonymous proverb rather than a named author, so I have left suggested_reattribution null.

results.earliest_print_source: Death Comes for the Archbishop, Willa Cather, 1927
results.notes: A genuine line from Cather's novel Death Comes for the Archbishop (1927), spoken in the context of the book's discussion of miracles and perception. Original reads without the comma: 'Where there is great love there are always miracles.' The corpus wording is otherwise faithful.

William Arthur Ward (1921-1994) was a prolific devotional aphorist — Fountains of Faith and widely syndicated maxims — and the 86,400-seconds gratitude line is attributed to him with unusual consistency across sources. But Ward's aphorisms circulate mostly through greeting-card and compilation channels without page citations, and I cannot place this one in a specific published collection. Note the author field gives 'William A. Ward'; the standard form is 'William Arthur Ward'.

Barclay, the Scottish theologian and commentator, is the most plausible claimant and this fits his homiletic register. Important context: the better-known variant ('The two most important days in your life are the day you are born and the day you find out why') is routinely credited to Mark Twain, and that Twain attribution is unsupported — no Twain source exists. So the Barclay line is the sounder of the two, but I still cannot point to a commentary or book where he wrote it.

results.earliest_print_source: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, William Blake, c. 1790-1793 ('Proverbs of Hell')
results.notes: A genuine Proverb of Hell from The Marriage of Heaven and Hell. Original: 'No bird soars too high, if he soars with his own wings.' Quoted here exactly.

results.earliest_print_source: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, William Blake, c. 1790-1793 (plate 14)
results.notes: Genuine Blake, from the 'printing house in Hell' passage on plate 14 of The Marriage of Heaven and Hell — the source Huxley took The Doors of Perception from. Wording here is accurate, including the archaic 'thro''. Blake's line continues '...of his cavern.' as given.

results.earliest_print_source: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, William Blake, c. 1790-1793 ('Proverbs of Hell')
results.notes: The attribution to Blake is correct, but the wording here is a modernized paraphrase. Blake's actual Proverb of Hell reads: 'If the fool would persist in his folly he would become wise.' The conditional subjunctive is doing real work in the original and is lost in the corpus version. Recommend correcting the text to Blake's wording, after which this would be a clean 'verified'.

Consistently credited to William Booth, founder of the Salvation Army, in Christian devotional compilations, and the paradox of power-through-surrender is squarely his theology. I have no primary source — no sermon, War Cry issue, or biography page — and Booth quotations in circulation are frequently secondhand recollections rather than documented text.

William Feather (1889-1981) was a Cleveland publisher who wrote aphorisms for his own periodical, The William Feather Magazine, and later collections — so unlike orphan proverbs, Feather attributions usually do trace back to a real author who published his own maxims. This line is attributed to him without competing claimants. I cannot cite the specific issue or collection, which keeps it under the bar.

Attributed to the antebellum Southern novelist and critic William Gilmore Simms in nineteenth-century quotation dictionaries and later compilations, and the sentiment and diction are period-appropriate for his critical prose. I cannot name the essay or volume it comes from, so no print source is given.

Almost certainly not William Gilmore Simms, who died in 1870. This passage is unmistakably modern therapeutic self-help prose — 'authentic experience of love', 'activates this inner being', 'the lover within', plus the anachronistic 'drive a certain car'. An automobile reference alone rules out a nineteenth-century author. The style closely matches contemporary daily-inspiration writing of the DailyOM sort, but I will not name an author I cannot confirm. Recommend rejecting the Simms attribution outright; this looks like a quote-site database collision, possibly compounded by the adjacent genuine Simms entry (q_1451).

William H. Danforth, founder of Ralston Purina, wrote the motivational classic I Dare You! (1931), and this line's goal-setting rhetoric fits that book's idiom, so it is a plausible source. I cannot confirm the sentence appears there, and business-motivation quotes of this vintage are frequently paraphrased or reassigned between authors in compilations.

This is the well-known prose poem 'My Symphony', attributed to the Unitarian minister William Henry Channing (1810-1884) in anthologies since the late nineteenth century — a long-standing and dominant attribution. Two cautions: it is regularly confused with his more famous uncle, William Ellery Channing, and some reference works treat the authorship as traditional rather than documented. The corpus text also reads 'to listen to stars and birds'; the familiar wording is 'to listen to stars and birds, to babes and sages, with open heart'.

Widely credited to William James and popularized further by its use in modern devotional writing. It circulates in several wordings ('The greatest use of a life is to spend it for something that will outlast it'), which is a warning sign, and I cannot locate it in James's published works, essays, or letters from memory. Plausible but unverified; the variant-wording spread suggests secondhand transmission rather than a quoted text.

Strongly doubtful as William James. 'Stress' in the psychological sense used here is a mid-twentieth-century coinage — Hans Selye's work from the 1930s onward — and would have been anachronistic for James, who died in 1910; he wrote about strain, worry, and habit, not 'stress'. The sentence also has the compressed, modern self-help cadence of a wellness-poster line rather than James's prose. I know of no source in his writings. Recommend dropping the James attribution; true origin unknown.

results.earliest_print_source: "Is Life Worth Living?" (address, 1895), collected in The Will to Believe and Other Essays in Popular Philosophy, William James, 1897
results.notes: Genuine James. The canonical wording is 'Believe that life is worth living, and your belief will help create the fact.' The corpus text drops 'help' and inserts 'your' before 'life' — a very common softening. Attribution is not in doubt; the wording should be corrected to the published form if the corpus cares about exactness.

Consistently attributed to James across quote dictionaries for many decades, and the register matches his prose on fatigue and effort (cf. 'The Energies of Men'). I cannot place it in a specific James text from memory, so no print citation is offered. Attribution plausible and stable, but unverified — deliberately below the promotion bar.

James genuinely wrote about the 'second wind' and habitual fatigue barriers in 'The Energies of Men' (1907), which is almost certainly the seed. But the second sentence — 'Give your dreams all you've got and you'll be amazed at the energy that comes out of you' — is mid-20th-century American motivational register, not James's 1907 prose. This reads as a self-help paraphrase grown onto a real James theme. Treat as unsourced.

results.earliest_print_source: The Principles of Psychology, William James, 1890, Vol. II (chapter on Reasoning)
results.notes: Genuine. James's sentence is 'the art of being wise is the art of knowing what to overlook.' The corpus text drops the second 'the art of'. Attribution solid; wording is a light trim of the original.

Long-standing and consistent attribution to Bryan in quote collections, and the cadence matches his oratory. I have a weak recollection that it comes from a turn-of-the-century Bryan address, but I cannot name the speech with confidence, so no citation is given. Frequently reproduced without source, which is the usual warning sign; still, no competing claimant is known to me.

Attributed to Penn very widely, but I cannot place it in Some Fruits of Solitude or any other Penn text I know. The same line circulates under Augustine and under Charles Spurgeon, which is the classic signature of a floating aphorism that later acquired a famous name. Uncertain enough that I will not name a true author.

results.earliest_print_source: As You Like It, William Shakespeare, c. 1599 (First Folio, 1623) — Act V, scene i, Touchstone
results.notes: Genuine Shakespeare, spoken by Touchstone to William. Text matches the received reading.

results.earliest_print_source: Twelfth Night, William Shakespeare, c. 1601 (First Folio, 1623) — Act IV, scene ii, Feste
results.notes: Genuine, but excerpted to the point of distortion: Feste's line is 'That that is, is; so I, being Master Parson, am Master Parson' — comic scholastic parody, not an aphorism about being. Attribution correct; the standalone fragment misrepresents the sense.

results.earliest_print_source: Hamlet, William Shakespeare, c. 1600 — Act II, scene ii, Hamlet to Rosencrantz
results.notes: Genuine, but misquoted. The text reads 'there is nothing either good or bad, but thinking makes it so.' The corpus version inserts 'in this world' and changes the construction. Recommend restoring the received wording.

Not Shakespeare — nothing in this diction, doctrine, or vocabulary belongs to him. This is classical Epicurean physics: nothing comes from nothing, things arise from 'seeds', and nothing perishes into nothing but dissolves back into its elements. That is the argument of Lucretius, De Rerum Natura, Book I, and 'seed' renders the Lucretian semina. Pliny the Elder states a close version in the Natural History, so I cannot be certain which classical author this English translation comes from, and I do not know the translator. Confident it is not Shakespeare; only probable that it is Lucretius.
results.suggested_reattribution: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura (probable; classical Epicurean source — not Shakespeare)

results.notes: Consistently attributed to William Temple, Archbishop of Canterbury, and consistent with his devotional writing of the 1930s (Christian Faith and Life, 1931, is the citation usually given, though I cannot confirm the page or that it is correct). Worth noting the neighbouring case: the popular 'Humility is not thinking less of yourself, but thinking of yourself less' is routinely misattributed to C. S. Lewis, who did not write it; this Temple passage is the older and better-grounded member of the family.

A well-known Churchill fake. It does not appear in the Churchill canon, and the International Churchill Society lists it among quotations he never said. Quote Investigator traced early forms to 1930s American motivational and advertising copy ('Success is never final and failure never fatal; it's courage that counts'), well before it was pinned to Churchill. I recall that provenance but will not present it as a citation. No true author identifiable.

Ubiquitously attributed to Churchill but never sourced. Langworth's Churchill by Himself does not locate it in any speech, letter, or book, and similar optimist/pessimist antitheses circulated before Churchill was attached to them. Plausible he said something like it in conversation; no evidence he did. Note this is a near-duplicate of q_1471 — the corpus should keep one.

results.earliest_print_source: Speech in the House of Commons, 28 October 1943 (Hansard), on rebuilding the bombed Commons Chamber
results.notes: Genuine and well documented — one of the Churchill quotations that actually survives checking. The recorded wording is 'We shape our buildings, and afterwards our buildings shape us.' The corpus text is the common paraphrase; consider restoring the Hansard wording.
Same unsourced Churchill attribution as q_1469, in the more idiomatic wording. No primary source exists in the Churchill canon. Duplicate of q_1469 — deduplicate before promotion.

A corrupted derivative. The line attributed to Churchill is about truth, not opportunity: 'Men occasionally stumble over the truth, but most of them pick themselves up and hurry off as if nothing ever happened.' Even that version is attributed rather than sourced to a document. This 'opportunity' rewrite has no standing at all; it is a motivational-poster mutation of the truth version.

A smoothed paraphrase. Churchill's documented sentiment is blunter: 'It is no use saying, "We are doing our best." You have got to succeed in doing what is necessary' — from his wartime remarks of the early 1940s. The polished 'It's not enough that we do our best; sometimes we have to do what's required' circulates without a source and appears to be a later rewrite. The idea is Churchill's; this wording is not established as his.

Not Churchill. Absent from the Churchill canon and listed by the International Churchill Society among quotations wrongly credited to him. The saying circulated in the early twentieth century before being attached to his name; it is also attributed to Norman MacEwan, though I cannot confirm that claim, so I am not naming a replacement author.

One of the most confidently repeated Churchill quotations he demonstrably never said. It appears in no speech, book, letter, or contemporary record; the International Churchill Society lists it as misattributed, and researchers have found no instance before the late twentieth century, decades after his death. Origin unknown.

results.earliest_print_source: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, Ludwig Wittgenstein, 1921 (German) / 1922 (English), proposition 6.4311
results.notes: Genuine, but truncated in a way that changes its force. The full proposition is conditional: 'If we take eternity to mean not infinite temporal duration but timelessness, then eternal life belongs to those who live in the present.' Stripped of the antecedent it reads as devotional advice rather than a claim about timelessness. Author field should be expanded to Ludwig Wittgenstein.

results.earliest_print_source: Address, "The Meaning of a Liberal Education," to the Federation of High School Teachers, New York, 9 January 1909
results.notes: Genuinely Wilson, and the standard citation given for it is the January 1909 address to the New York high school teachers, reproduced in The Papers of Woodrow Wilson. I am reporting that citation from training memory and have not confirmed it against the primary text, so treat the source line as strong-but-unchecked rather than as a verified page reference. Attribution itself is not seriously disputed.

Long attributed to Wilson and included in mainstream quotation dictionaries under his name, which is decent secondary evidence. I cannot name the speech or letter it comes from, so no citation is given. No competing claimant known to me.

results.earliest_print_source: Wumenguan (無門關, The Gateless Barrier), Wumen Huikai, 1228 — verse to Case 19, 'Ordinary Mind Is the Way'
results.notes: Genuine Wumen. The Chinese verse is 春有百花秋有月，夏有涼風冬有雪，若無閒事挂心頭，便是人間好時節 — Wumen's capping verse to the Nanquan koan in Case 19 of the Wumenguan. The English here is a loose modern rendering rather than a literal translation (this phrasing is generally Stephen Mitchell's), so the translator should be credited if the corpus tracks that. Attribution to Wumen is solid.

Attributed to Wumen and almost certainly one of his capping verses in the Wumenguan — the image is the standard one rendered elsewhere as 'It is too clear and so it is hard to see; a dunce once searched for fire with a lighted lantern — had he known what fire was, he could have cooked his rice sooner.' I cannot reliably name the case number, and the English is a modern paraphrase, so I am not supplying a citation. Attribution to Wumen is consistent across renderings; the specific source line is not established here.

Consistently attributed to Hakuun Yasutani (Yasutani Roshi) in Zen literature in English, where it circulates as a remark from his teaching rather than from a book he wrote — plausible, since his teaching reached print mainly through students. I associate it with the Kapleau/Three Pillars of Zen lineage of texts and with its use as an epigraph in later nature and Zen writing, but I cannot pin a first printing, so no citation is given. Attribution stable; sourcing unresolved.

Circulates in English-language collections of Yiddish proverbs, but I cannot place it in any specific anthology (Ayalti, Kumove, Rosten, etc.) from my training knowledge. Generic proverb attributions of this kind rarely have a traceable first appearance. No evidence it is NOT a Yiddish proverb either — just no confirmation.

results.earliest_print_source: Star Wars: Episode V — The Empire Strikes Back, screenplay by Leigh Brackett and Lawrence Kasdan, 1980
results.notes: Provenance is certain: Yoda's line to Luke on Dagobah in The Empire Strikes Back (1980), voiced by Frank Oz. IMPORTANT — the text as stored is a corruption. The canonical line is 'Do. Or do not. There is no try.' The stored 'Do or do not do. There is no try.' should be corrected. Confidence 0.9 rather than higher only because the wording deviates; the source itself is unambiguous. Note that the words were written by the screenwriters, not spoken by a historical person.

Not a recognized translation of any sutra I can pin down. The sense plausibly corresponds to Yoga Sutra I.16 (para-vairagya: dispassion arising from discernment of purusha, the true self, leaving one untroubled by the gunas), but the English is a loose modern paraphrase rather than a standard rendering. The feminine pronouns suggest a deliberately gender-inclusive modern translation or a paraphrase collection; I cannot identify which, and will not guess. Attribution to the Yoga Sutras is plausible but the specific wording is unverified.

This maps closely and specifically to Yoga Sutra IV.2 — 'jatyantara-parinamah prakrty-apurat' — the transformation into another state of being comes about through the filling-in/overflowing of prakriti (nature). 'Change into a new state of being' = jatyantara-parinama; 'fullness of nature' = prakrty-apura. The underlying source text is therefore identifiable with reasonable confidence, but the English is an unidentified modern translation and I will not name a translator or edition I cannot confirm. Held below 0.8 for that reason.

Yogi Amrit Desai (founder of Kripalu Center) is a real teacher and this is consistent with his idiom, but I cannot place the line in any of his books, talks, or in a Kripalu publication from training knowledge. It circulates mainly on quote sites and yoga-studio ephemera, which is weak evidence. Plausible but unconfirmed.

Berra used the line and claimed it in 'The Yogi Book: I Really Didn't Say Everything I Said!' (1998), so the attribution is not baseless — but the saying substantially predates him. It is commonly traced to Paul Valery, who wrote in the 1930s that the future 'is no longer what it used to be' (Regards sur le monde actuel), and English instances appear well before Berra's career-quote fame. Berra is the popularizer, not the originator. Confidence here reflects confidence in the attribution AS GIVEN, which is weak; my confidence in the earlier-origin finding is considerably higher. I have not confirmed a page/edition for the Valery line and so leave the print source null.
results.suggested_reattribution: Paul Valery (earlier form, 1930s); popularized in English by Yogi Berra

results.earliest_print_source: The Gateless Gate (Wumenguan / Mumonkan), Wumen Huikai, 1228 — case 19, closing verse
results.notes: This is the second half of Wumen Huikai's verse to Case 19 of the Wumenguan ('Ordinary Mind is the Way'): 'Hundreds of flowers in spring, the moon in autumn, a cool breeze in summer, snow in winter. If your mind isn't clouded by unnecessary things, this is the best season of your life.' (若無閑事挂心頭，便是人間好時節). Not Yunmen Wenyan — the confusion likely arises because Yunmen is the source of the similar-sounding 'Every day is a good day' (Blue Cliff Record, case 6). I am confident in this reattribution.
results.suggested_reattribution: Wumen Huikai (Mumon Ekai), The Gateless Gate, case 19 verse

results.notes: Not an anonymous proverb — this is Matsuo Basho, from the short prose piece commonly translated as 'Words by a Brushwood Gate' (Saimon no ji): 'Do not seek to follow in the footsteps of the men of old; seek what they sought.' The rendering in wide English circulation comes largely through Robert Aitken's 'A Zen Wave: Basho's Haiku and Zen' (1978); I recall the attribution firmly but not the exact page, so I leave the print source field null rather than guess an edition.

This is a line from the Xinxin Ming (Hsin Hsin Ming, 'Verses on the Faith Mind') traditionally attributed to Jianzhi Sengcan, the Third Chan Patriarch (d. 606): 不用求真，唯須息見 — 'Do not seek the truth; only cease to cherish opinions.' Genuinely Zen, so the category label is not wrong, but a specific text and author are identifiable and should replace 'Zen proverb'. Traditional authorship of the Xinxin Ming is itself disputed by scholars (the text is likely later than Sengcan), which is why I do not go higher.

A widely circulated Zen saying whose textual origin I cannot establish. It is often reproduced in English-language Zen anthologies and in Alan Watts-influenced literature, and it may derive from a Zenrin Kushu couplet, but I cannot confirm a Chinese or Japanese original or a first English printing. Honest unknown.

A fragment of a longer saying that circulates in several forms ('When you seek it, you cannot find it... when you no longer seek it, it is always with you'). I cannot place it in any Chan or Zen text I know, and the short form given here has no traceable source. Treat as unsourced.

The diction ('ten thousand questions... cut through the one question') strongly resembles the teaching idiom of Korean Son master Seung Sahn, whose talks and letters ('Dropping Ashes on the Buddha', 'The Compass of Zen') repeatedly reduce all questions to one 'don't know' question. I am not confident enough to name him as the source, so I leave the reattribution null per the rules. Not an anonymous traditional proverb, in any case — it reads as a 20th-century teacher's phrasing.

Genuinely traditional: half of the well-known Chan couplet 竹密不妨流水過，山高豈礙白雲飛 — 'However dense the bamboo, it does not stop the water flowing through; however high the mountain, it does not hinder the white clouds from drifting past.' The couplet is collected in the Zenrin Kushu (the Japanese anthology of Chan sayings) and appears in Chan recorded-sayings literature. 'Zen proverb' is an accurate attribution. I do not cite a specific edition/date for the Zenrin Kushu because I am not sure enough of its compilation and printing dates to state them.

No basis in any Chan or Zen text I know. The five-step 'look to / follow / walk with / see through / become the master' progression is a modern Western self-development formulation of the kind that gets a 'Zen proverb' label attached to it on quote sites. Zen literature tends in the opposite direction on this theme (see Basho's 'seek what they sought', or Linji's 'if you meet the Buddha, kill him'). Recommend treating as unsourced modern coinage.

results.earliest_print_source: If You Meet the Buddha on the Road, Kill Him!, Sheldon B. Kopp, 1972
results.notes: This is an item from Sheldon Kopp's 'An Eschatological Laundry List: A Partial Register of the 927 (or was it 928?) Eternal Truths', the closing list of his 1972 book. The book's Zen-flavored title (from the Linji koan) is very likely why items from that list drifted into circulation as 'Zen proverbs'. I recall this specific item with reasonable confidence; I do not recall a page number and so do not give one.

Not traceable to any Zen text I know. It has the aphoristic register of Sheldon Kopp's 'Eschatological Laundry List' (1972), which is the demonstrable source of at least one neighboring 'Zen proverb' in this batch, but I cannot confirm this line is on that list and will not assert it. Unsourced.

I cannot place this in Chan or Zen literature. The formulation reads more like Western philosophical idealism (the Hegelian claim that the infinite is not something set apart from the finite) than a translated Buddhist source, though the sentiment is compatible with Mahayana non-duality. Origin unknown; the 'Zen proverb' label is unsupported.

A genuine traditional Chan/Zen maxim: 大疑大悟，小疑小悟，不疑不悟. It is strongly associated with Hakuin Ekaku (1686-1769), who quoted and expanded on it constantly ('beneath great doubt lies great awakening'), but it predates him in Chinese Chan — versions are attributed to Song-era masters such as Mengshan Deyi and appear in Boshan's exhortations on rousing doubt. So 'Zen proverb' is defensible as an attribution; if a person is wanted, Hakuin is the popularizer rather than the originator. Held below 0.8 because I cannot cite a specific text and edition.

results.earliest_print_source: The Way of Zen, Alan W. Watts, 1957
results.notes: A real Zenrin Kushu couplet — 兀然無事坐，春來草自青 — made famous in English by Alan Watts, who renders it in 'The Way of Zen' (1957) as 'Sitting quietly, doing nothing, / Spring comes, and the grass grows by itself.' The stored text ('Sitting peacefully') is a variant of Watts' wording; consider normalizing to the standard rendering. 'Zen proverb' is an accurate attribution for the underlying couplet; Watts is the English source.

Corresponds to the common Chan phrase 好事不如無 — literally 'a good thing is not as good as nothing', i.e. better no affairs at all. It is a stock phrase in Chan recorded sayings and koan-collection commentary and appears in Zen phrase anthologies, so the 'Zen proverb' label is accurate in substance. I cannot identify the earliest text, so I stay well below the promotion bar.

The idea is authentically Huayan/Chan (一即一切，一切即一 — 'one is all, all is one', which appears in the Xinxin Ming and pervades Huayan thought), but this specific English sentence is not a recognized translation of any line I can identify. Likely a modern paraphrase of that doctrine rather than a quotation. Attribution to a Zen text is unverified.

results.earliest_print_source: Transformations of Consciousness, Ken Wilber, Jack Engler & Daniel P. Brown, 1986
results.notes: This is Jack Engler's well-known formulation from his work on the interface of psychoanalytic developmental theory and Buddhist meditation: 'You have to be somebody before you can be nobody.' It first appeared in his 1984 Journal of Transpersonal Psychology essay on therapeutic aims in psychotherapy and meditation, reprinted in 'Transformations of Consciousness' (1986). Its Buddhist subject matter is why it gets relabeled a Zen proverb; it is a 20th-century academic coinage, not a traditional saying. I am confident about Engler and the essay, less so about exact bibliographic details.

Widely reproduced as a 'Zen proverb' on quote sites, and occasionally attached to Emerson or to unnamed 'Chinese proverb' labels, which is itself a sign of a floating attribution. I cannot place it in any Zen text or trace a first printing. The aphorism's shape (a neat English epigram with a single ironic turn) suggests a Western origin. Unsourced.

The doctrine is authentic — the Vimalakirti Sutra's 心淨則佛土淨 ('when the mind is pure, the buddha-land is pure') is the classic statement, echoed in the Platform Sutra — but this English sentence is not a translation of any passage I can identify, and 'heart' for mind/citta suggests a loose modern rendering. Genuinely Buddhist in sense, unverified as a quotation.

This line circulates very widely and is most often credited to the Lankavatara Sutra; it is also quoted freely in Zen contexts and in Western Buddhist writing. I recall the Lankavatara association clearly but cannot confirm the passage or a translation (Suzuki's 1932 English version is the usual candidate), so I do not assert the reattribution. The tetralemma structure ('not as they seem, nor otherwise') is characteristic of Madhyamaka/Yogacara phrasing, which makes a sutra origin plausible rather than certain.

As a generic 'Zen saying' this is untraceable — it is a three-word English phrase, not a rendering of a known koan, sutra line, or classical Chan formula I can place. The reason it circulates in English is Shunryu Suzuki: 'Not always so' is remembered by his San Francisco Zen Center students as one of his habitual correctives, and it supplies the title of the posthumous collection 'Not Always So: Practicing the True Spirit of Zen' (Suzuki, edited by Edward Espe Brown, HarperCollins, 2002), drawn from lectures given in the late 1960s and early 1970s. I am confident that book and title exist; I cannot pin the phrase to a specific dated lecture or to any pre-Suzuki print occurrence, so I am not recording an earliest print source. Suggesting Suzuki as the proximate English source rather than an anonymous tradition, but flagging that he was himself gesturing at a general Zen attitude, so 'Zen saying' is loose rather than flatly wrong.

Not Zen. This is the signature doctrine of the Ming neo-Confucian Wang Yangming (1472-1529), the unity of knowing and acting (zhi xing he yi), stated in the Chuanxi lu / 'Instructions for Practical Living' roughly as: there have never been people who know and do not act; those who know but do not act simply do not yet know. The English wording here matches the paraphrase popularized in Western business and self-help writing — Stephen Covey used a near-identical line ('To know and not to do is really not to know') in The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989), which is likely how it entered circulation with a vague Eastern-wisdom label that later hardened into 'Zen saying'. I am confident about the Wang Yangming doctrine and reasonably confident about the Covey transmission path; I am not confident enough about which translation produced this exact English sentence to name an earliest print source, so I am leaving that null rather than guessing at a Wing-tsit Chan page.
results.suggested_reattribution: Wang Yangming (paraphrase; popularized in English via Stephen Covey)

results.earliest_print_source: Dust Tracks on a Road, Zora Neale Hurston, 1942
results.notes: Correctly attributed. 'Research is formalized curiosity. It is poking and prying with a purpose' is Hurston's, from her autobiography Dust Tracks on a Road (J. B. Lippincott, 1942), in the material on her anthropological fieldwork. The trailing sentence — 'It is a seeking that he who wishes may know the cosmic secrets of the world and they that dwell therein' — is also Hurston's voice and also from Dust Tracks, but I recall it sitting in the book's concluding passage rather than immediately adjoining the 'formalized curiosity' lines. So the author and the book are solid; the quote as presented may be a splice of two nearby-but-not-contiguous sentences. Holding confidence at 0.85 rather than higher for that reason. Recommend a human check against the 1942 text before treating this as a continuous quotation, and consider trimming to the first two sentences, which are the securely contiguous part.
